title: Ebola outbreak passes 10,000 cases in DRC after nurse killed, another injured
text:
More than 10,000 people have been infected with Ebola virus in what is now the Democratic Republic of Congo's (DRC) largest outbreak on record.

There have been 4,887 deaths across eight provinces in the DRC since the outbreak was declared in mid-May.

Responding to the DRC's largest Ebola outbreak Amid the largest Ebola virus outbreak recorded in the DRC's history, healthcare workers try to keep the system running.

It is now the second largest Ebola virus outbreak globally, and the fastest growing in the DRC's history, according to local health officials.

More than 2,700 of those infected are children, along with hundreds of the dead, non-profit organisation Save the Children told the ABC.

The organisation's DRC director, Greg Ramm, said the grim milestone was a "stark reminder of the scale of this crisis".

"Behind this milestone are thousands of families facing unimaginable fear and uncertainty, and children are bearing some of the heaviest consequences," he said.

"This outbreak is unfolding in communities already affected by conflict, displacement and food insecurity.

Ebola treatment centres have been established across the affected region. (AP Photo: Sebastien Kitsa Musayi)

"Families are struggling to access health care, health facilities are under immense pressure, and many communities lack the resources needed to prevent transmission and keep children safe."

Unlike previous Ebola outbreaks, this time transmission comes from the rarer Bundibugyo Ebola virus.

Bundibugyo did not show up on available Ebola testing kits for weeks, and there is no available vaccine for it.

Ebola cases rise to eight in Kenya A person who had contact with Kenya's first Ebola victim becomes the country's eighth case of the deadly virus.

Earlier this month, two countries, Kenya and Nigeria, reported their first cases linked to the ongoing outbreak.

A patient in Nigeria, identified as the Ugandan-born wife of a Swiss diplomat, was flown to Switzerland for treatment on Monday, local time.

Kenyan officials reported their second Bundibugyo death on Tuesday, with almost 100 close contacts of other cases remaining in quarantine.

In response, the Africa Centres for Disease Control and Prevention (Africa CDC) has scheduled a high-level virtual meeting of African ministers of health on Wednesday.

Africa CDC's director-general, Jean Kaseya, said their response "must move faster".

"Ebola is crossing borders," Dr Kaseya said.

"We have the expertise and the capacity on this continent. We must mobilise them together to stop this outbreak and save lives."

Multiple African countries have since recorded cases. (Reuters: Sodiq Adelakun )

Neighbouring Uganda has banned all non-essential travel to and from the DRC, and its returning citizens will be ordered to quarantine for 21 days.

Nurse killed while treating DRC Ebola patients

Late last week, a nurse was killed and a health worker severely injured while responding to an Ebola alert in the DRC's Tshopo province.

The incident was announced by World Health Organization (WHO) director-general Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus.

The race against time to contain Ebola Tensions are running high as officials fight to stop the rapid spread of Ebola in the Democratic Republic of Congo, where aid workers tell the ABC they are already playing catch-up with the deadly disease.

"Everyone working to protect communities from this deadly disease must be able to work in dignity and safety," he said in a post on X.

The DRC's eastern region, the epicentre of the outbreak, where 28 out of 36 health zones have recorded cases, is one of the most unstable areas in the world.

Those working on the ground have told the ABC they face violence, threats and conspiracy theories while fighting to contain the outbreak.

The WHO's regional director for Africa, Mohamed Janabi, also condemned the attack.

"Those responding to the Ebola outbreak must be protected," Professor Janabi said.

title: Fox axing from Devils VFL not due to single incident, club says
text:
Tasmania Devils have strongly defended their club culture after axing VFL skipper Robbie Fox following an off-field indiscretion.

The Devils also said the decision to part ways with their inaugural captain was not based on an isolated incident.

The team confirmed yesterday that Fox would not be offered a contract for the 2027 season, citing, in part, the club's "expectations regarding player behaviour and adherence to our standards".

Yesterday, the ABC revealed Fox had been involved in an incident at a Hobart pub, the Granada Tavern, where he was ejected from the venue after becoming drunk and disorderly, and acting belligerently toward some staff.

It is also understood a bottle was thrown and smashed during the incident.

Nobody is believed to have been injured, and there was no police involvement.

The ABC can also reveal Fox had earlier played in a charity golf event at the nearby Claremont Golf Club with several Devils teammates.

Fox's foursome included vice-captain Jye Menzie and reigning best-and-fairest Hugh Dixon.

There is no suggestion those players were involved in the later incident at the Granada Tavern.

Robbie Fox (left) pictured during his tenure with the Swans. (Getty Images: AFL Photos/Michael Willson)

Chief marketing officer Kath McCann told local media today that the decision not to offer Fox a contract was, in part, the culmination of several "situations".

"I want to be really clear that there was no particular one incident that led to this decision", she said.

"There have been situations where Robbie probably had some areas for improvement and for growth, and he's dealing with the consequences of that.

"I think it's fair to say that not everybody gets everything right," she said

Fox has been contacted for comment.

Ms McCann said the Devils's culture was strong, and that their swift decision to cut on-field ties with Fox was indicative of that.

"Our club has really high standards, and we're really proud of that," she said.

"We've said from the start that our club is focused on ensuring we work with the very best people, and the highest of standards.

" It's been a part of our success to date and will continue to be in the future. "

But McCann also confirmed that Fox would continue in his role as the club's Strategic Projects Lead, and defended the decision to keep him on as a club employee.

She said the club was "very comfortable" with where it had landed regarding his playing contract and that it would not divulge details around its internal processes.

"Robbie's a member of our staff, he's been an important part of our inaugural year, and he's a really great person," she said.

Fox played 13 games for the Devils in an injury-affected year, after being recruited back to his native Tasmania following his delisting by the Sydney Swans.

Under his captaincy, the Devils finished in the VFL top four and earned a finals double chance.

A council whose mayor resigned on Wednesday morning has held a bizarre press conference, with the chief executive saying she did not know the mayor had officially stepped down, and the acting mayor had not read her allegations of bullying. Jos Mitchell resigned from her role at Redlands City Council, on Brisbane’s bayside, alleging it was a toxic workplace that had a detrimental impact on her health. Mitchell had been on sick leave since May, and in a statement said she had recently undergone surgery and was suffering from an autoimmune disease. Deputy Mayor Julie Talty and council CEO Louise Rusan initially said the mayor had not officially resigned. Julius Dennis Deputy Mayor Julie Talty, who had been acting mayor while Mitchell was on leave, fronted media with Redlands chief executive Louise Rusan at 11.30am, insisting it was business as usual for the council.

“We understand there’s been some statements in the media by our mayor, Jos Mitchell, in regards to her intention to resign her position,” Talty said. “At this stage, we’ve not had any formal confirmation of that, so we’ll continue to support the mayor until she does give us that confirmation.” Jos Mitchell had been on leave since May 11. Dan Peled Talty said she had not read the comments made by Mitchell online, so she could not speak to them. Rusan began her statement by saying it was “business as usual” at the council, but was pressed by journalists about screenshots of an email sent to her by Mitchell tendering her resignation at 5am.

She was pulled to the side by an adviser before returning to the microphones. “I’ve just received advice that we’ve received a resignation, right this moment,” Rusan said. “So up until two seconds ago, I had not had any contact with the mayor.” Rusan insisted the council had a “wonderful” culture, but would not speak directly about the allegations by Mitchell of a smear campaign. “I believe we have a very good culture here at Redland City Council,” she said.

An hour and a half after the presser, the council put out an official media release acknowledging Mitchell’s resignation. “The Office of Mayor at Redland City Council has become vacant, triggering a by-election to elect a new Mayor of Redland City,” it read. The strange press conference took place outside the council building. Matt Dennien It said Talty would remain as acting mayor until a by-election was held by the Electoral Commission of Queensland. “On behalf of Council, I wish the former mayor all the best for the future,” Talty said.

Speaking in parliament on Wednesday afternoon, local government minister Ann Leahy said her department would work with the commission to organise an election. She ensured that it would not occur during the Christmas period, but didn’t clarify if the vote would be held sooner, or pushed into next year. Ann Leahy addressed the situation in parliament. Jamila Filippone “A key priority throughout this process is to ensure the residents of the Redlands community have a local government that works for them,” Leahy said. “I would encourage anyone considering standing for election as mayor to understand the commitment to the community that such a role entails.”

A nationwide review of biosecurity measures will target the imported red fire ant incursion in Sydney’s inner west after revelations the location of the nest was only required to be checked every three years. A biosecurity control order is in place to limit the movement of high-risk goods after the established fire ant nest was discovered in Enfield Intermodal Logistics Centre in September, and the public was notified two weeks ago. The established fire ant nest was discovered under concrete. NSW Government A review by the inspector-general of biosecurity will examine the Sydney nest as a first case study in a broad assessment of biosecurity policies. In the past three years, more than 160 ant lures were deployed around the Enfield site and until September did not detect any fire ants. While some of the businesses at the logistics centre were considered higher risk and monitored more frequently, under current policies the location where the nest was discovered only required checking every three years.

Advertisement

Invasive Species Council advocacy director Reece Pianta said: “The current biosecurity arrangements clearly do not reflect biological reality and they need to be urgently changed.” Pianta said he hoped the review would provide recommendations to strengthen the biosecurity system to prevent fire ants from establishing elsewhere in Australia. Reece Pianta (left) a fire ant expert at the Invasive Species Council, and local resident and fire ants activist Stuart Webber, inspect a fire ants mound in a horse paddock in Queensland. Dan Peled An interim report, to be made public by April, will examine the management of the biosecurity risk at sites such as Enfield, including surveillance arrangements, according to a document outlining the approach of the inspector-general’s review. After the interim report is delivered, the broader review will look at other cases around the country to determine if the current approaches to risk management and information sharing are adequate to protect Australia’s biosecurity.

Advertisement

The Sydney nest is thought to have been more than a year old when it was discovered, and the ants’ country of origin remains unknown. As nests mature in six months, at which point queen ants can fly to other locations, this would have given the ants time to establish themselves in other locations. Related Article Environmental threats ‘It can get worse’: The bite that burns like fire and killed a football hero A control order now covers a two-kilometre radius around the Enfield nest site, which requires businesses that move soil, mulch, turf, potted plants and heavy equipment to take special precautions before transporting the items outside the controlled zone. More than 400 calls from members of the public have been made to the government’s fire ant hotline, but no further signs of the deadly pest have been confirmed. A team of 60 officers and nine sniffer dogs have combed nearby parks, streets and schools and found no further nests. Fire ants are one of the world’s worst invasive species and responsible for at least 80 deaths in the United States.

The painful bite can kill pets and native wildlife and can be deadly for humans sensitive to insect bites. The bite triggers a burning sensation for up to an hour and can create unsightly pustules on the skin. The unravelling housing crisis confronting Sydney makes the proposal by NSW Opposition Leader Kellie Sloane to shut Long Bay prison and convert the prime government-owned coastal location into 12,000 new homes worth considering. The Coalition looked at the site a decade ago when the then corrections minister David Elliott said that “prisoners should not have access to such prime Sydney real estate at the expense of taxpayers” and advocated the sale of the jail for housing. The NSW Liberals announced plans to close the Long Bay Correctional Complex to make way for housing. Sitthixay Ditthavong His Coalition government failed to act. But 13 months ago, the opposition revisited the sale, and Sloane has relaunched the idea with the proposal to establish a Long Bay Delivery Authority to relocate the prison, inmates and staff to existing regional and metropolitan centres. Sloane told the Urban Development Institute of Australia’s state conference on Wednesday that the aim was not to create luxury housing: “Young people are sick of hearing governments say housing plans are about delivering more homes for young people, only for those homes to end up being luxury apartments they can’t afford.”

Advertisement

Labor is vigorously opposing the sale. Planning Minister Paul Scully labelled it a fantasy. “The reality is the idea of putting 12,000 homes on the site behind us would create an area of around three times the density of Green Square without any of the transport infrastructure. This doesn’t pass the most basic of planning tests,” he said. The NSW government talks a lot about housing. It’s Premier Chris Minns’ signature policy. His rezoning reforms were aimed eventually at delivering 170,000 new homes. But, three years later, NSW lags long behind National Housing Accord targets. The opposition’s rejuvenated Long Bay plan is an early glimpse of the March state election campaign, with the major parties playing tit-for-tat on housing policy in each other’s safe seats. Labor proposes massive developments offering some 9400 new homes in Woollahra and Edgecliff, located in Sloane’s seat of Vaucluse, while the opposition’s Long Bay announcement has targeted Attorney General Michael Daley’s seat of Maroubra.

Advertisement

Scully is not wrong in pointing out the transport infrastructure problems particular to developing Long Bay. Related Article Exclusive

NSW Votes ‘Not another suburb for luxury housing’: Liberals to unveil Long Bay housing plan However, the minister has apparently forgotten that long before the closure developed into a political arm-wrestle, an Infrastructure NSW report in 2014 identified a light rail extension from Kingsford to La Perouse, including a stop at Long Bay, to unlock potential land use. In 2020, the South East Sydney Transport Strategy recommended a metro line be investigated to La Perouse, although another metro is unlikely until Metro West is finished and the state’s balance sheet improves. Sloane said that the Long Bay Delivery Authority would be set up within 100 days of the Coalition winning government. It would consider how best to relocate Long Bay’s 1200 prisoners and 1000 staff while retaining a city-based jail facility close enough for ease of access for families and the workforce. The Coalition must answer the valid questions about accessibility, the rehoming of prisoners and how it would preserve heritage aspects of the 1909-built jail.

title: Forget the mortgage belt: Gamers are getting smashed and Chalmers should worry
text:

Analysis PoliticsFederalInflation Forget the mortgage belt: Gamers are getting smashed and Chalmers should worry Shane Wright October 28, 2026 — 3:51pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Put aside your pity for those with a mortgage or people struggling to put food on the table. It’s the gamers who are being hit by inflation. And as gamers deal with huge spikes in the prices of their consoles, the policy problems facing the Reserve Bank, Jim Chalmers and the phalanx of state and territory treasurers follow. Chalmers and Finance Minister Katy Gallagher have to use their upcoming budget update to actually reduce spending. Aresna Villanueva The latest monthly inflation figures from the bureau of statistics all-but guaranteed that the Reserve Bank’s monetary policy committee will inflict another rate rise on the economy on Melbourne Cup Day. The 4.3 per cent headline inflation rate for September, and 3.6 per cent for the key underlying measure were, as the bank’s deputy governor Andrew Hauser said, too high.

Advertisement

As Hauser and governor Michele Bullock have often reminded Australians, the RBA has only one tool to deal with inflation. Hence its four rate rises this year, with the big chance of another that will push the cash rate to an 18-year high of 4.85 per cent next Tuesday. By lifting rates, the bank is trying to reduce overall demand across the economy with the stated aim of bringing inflation back to its 2-3 per cent target – something it has spectacularly failed to do since the final days of the Abbott government – by the end of next year. It can definitely be assisted by a reduction in government spending, at the federal and state level. Chalmers and Finance Minister Katy Gallagher have to use their upcoming budget update to actually reduce spending.

Advertisement

No matter how they characterise the pressures on government services, a budget deficit of $31.5 billion (after a $22.3 billion shortfall in 2025-26) is a loosening of monetary policy during a period of excess demand in the economy. Related Article Inflation Inflation jumps to 4.3 per cent, fuelling prospect of Cup Day rate rise Their state counterparts, many of whom seem to believe their job is to ignore their role in the economy while putting out their hands for more federal cash, have to dramatically lift their performances and tighten their belts. They have to make some tough decisions because of two other issues at play and directly outside government control. The first is the war started by Donald Trump against Iran. Brent crude started the year at $US60 a barrel. On Wednesday, it was $US115.

Advertisement

For the past two months, it has averaged above $US100 a barrel. This spike is feeding through the global economy, from bowsers to PVC pipes to agricultural fertilisers, and is one of the reasons that central banks everywhere are lifting their interest rates. The second big factor is the one that is hurting the struggling gamers. The AI construction boom is lifting business investment and pitting tech firms against each other in a semiconductor and chip war. That war has spilt over into the broader economy. The price of the next Nintendo Switch is going to soar. The September inflation figures showed the costs of games and toys have climbed 15.5 per cent over the past 12 months. Only petrol and diesel have gone up by more.

Advertisement

It’s the biggest increase in games and toys on record and is because demand for computer chips in games and consoles is running much, much faster than supply. Prices for computer equipment, which fell 91 per cent through the first 25 years of this century, have climbed by 6.3 per cent over the past 12 months. It’s why the price of a Nintendo Switch 2 has climbed by 10 per cent this year. Why the Sony PS5 is up by 20 per cent. A MacBook Neo by 17 per cent. iPhones and iPads are going up by even more. The inflation figures were released around the same time that SK Hynix, one of the world’s biggest producers of computer chips and semiconductors, released its third quarter earnings report. It showed average selling prices of its key products had climbed by 20 per cent over the past three months and up four-fold since last year. And it’s not going to get any better.

Advertisement

Company chief financial officer Kim Woo-hyun warned huge demand from across the world meant supply shortages were likely to “persist through to 2030”. Gamers will have to go back to playing pick-up-sticks or dust-encrusted versions of Squatter if that comes to pass. Treasury secretary Jenny Wilkinson, who sits on the Reserve Bank’s monetary policy committee, on Wednesday noted that the data centre building boom is competing for labour and resources with government infrastructure projects and the housing sector. We don’t have to go back far in time to see what that situation means for ongoing inflation. Just look at the early 2000s mining boom. Chalmers, Gallagher and Anthony Albanese are now clearly on notice that they have to play a larger role in easing demand in the Australian economy to deal with global inflationary pressures. Aspiring gold producer Forrestania Resources has firmed up another piece of its production puzzle, tabling a new mineral resource estimate for its recently acquired Symes Find gold deposit in Western Australia’s Wheatbelt region. The updated JORC-compliant resource clocks in at 803,600 tonnes grading one gram per tonne (g/t) gold for 25,800 ounces using a 0.5g/t cut-off grade. Forrestania’s Symes Find deposit, located in Western Australia’s Wheatbelt region, is set to provide ore to the Edna May production hub (pictured). The new resource defines what’s left in the ground after previous owner, mid-tier producer Ramelius Resources, mined 42,000 ounces of higher-grade 2.41g/t gold from the deposit’s open pits in 2024. Notably, the ore was trucked 121 kilometres to the Edna May processing plant, which Forrestania now owns. Forrestania acquired the project as part of the package from Ramelius in September. The resource is broken down into 220,000 tonnes at 0.83g/t gold in the high-confidence measured category, 406,900 tonnes at 1.07g/t in the indicated category and 176,700 tonnes at 1.07g/t gold in the inferred category.

Advertisement

‘Symes Find is an excellent example of Forrestania’s strategy of acquiring advanced gold assets within trucking distance of Edna May.’ Forrestania Resources chairman David Geraghty Importantly, more than 75 per cent of the remaining gold ounces sit in the higher-confidence measured and indicated categories, giving Forrestania a solid handle on the deposit’s remaining riches as it pushes ahead with mining studies. The resource update comes as the company ticks off a series of important milestones at the Edna May operation, putting it on a fast track to restart gold production in mid-December. As a tangible sign of confidence in its production readiness, Forrestania has already delivered the first ore from its nearby Johnson Range mine to the Edna May run-of-mine pad. Forrestania Resources chairman David Geraghty said: “Symes Find is an excellent example of Forrestania’s strategy of acquiring advanced gold assets within trucking distance of Edna May. Following successful mining from the deposit, this updated resource confirms a meaningful remaining gold inventory and further strengthens Forrestania’s pipeline of future production opportunities as we move toward first gold at Edna May in December 2026.” The Edna May restart will mark a big step in Forrestania’s strategy to build a leading Western Australian gold business using a classic hub-and-spoke model, underpinned by its two strategic processing hubs. While all eyes are on the imminent Edna May restart, the company is also rapidly pushing ahead with refurbishment of its second hub at Lake Johnston, slated for commissioning and production in early 2027.

Advertisement

Forrestania has been quietly assembling a significant inventory of ore sources to feed its two hubs, building a global mineral resource inventory that now tops two million ounces. The tally includes the recently acquired 223,300-ounce Tampia project along with its Tycho, British Hills and Johnson Range deposits. The company’s restart timetable is emerging against a strong Australian gold backdrop, with spot prices consolidating around a handsome A$6000 per ounce, providing a powerful commercial tailwind for its production ambitions. In other news today, Forrestania has drawn a line in the sand on its takeover of Zenith Minerals, confirming its offer, first launched on June 9, will close at 5pm (AWST) on November 12. The company says it will not extend the now-unconditional offer unless its hand is forced under section 624(2) of the Corporations Act 2001, which provides for an automatic extension in certain circumstances. With 62.04 per cent of Zenith already in its grasp, Forrestania appears firmly in the driver’s seat as it eyes the 90 per cent ownership threshold generally required to pursue compulsory acquisition and lock away another piece of its broader WA gold consolidation strategy. With first ore already on the ground at Edna May and a new parcel of ounces confirmed at Symes Find, Forrestania looks to be methodically de-risking its production plans. As the final pieces fall into place for a pre-Christmas restart at Edna May and Lake Johnston making rapid progress towards its 2027 start-up, the two-hub strategy is edging closer to reality, setting the stage for the company to establish itself as a serious new force in WA’s gold sector. Passengers on a luxury ship touring the world have been told their unexpected final stop is Cambodia after the cruise company suspended operations, citing “extraordinary” fuel costs. Florida-based Villa Vie Residences’ 650-passenger ship Odyssey is now moored in Sihanoukville, Cambodia, and the company “is working with residents to co-ordinate disembarkation and identify temporary living arrangements”, according to a statement on Wednesday AEST. The Villa Vie Odyssey’s luxury odyssey has come to an unexpected end. nna\april.glover While the company is covering lodging and local transportation, it hasn’t provided funding for passengers to depart the country, Villa Vie Founder Mikael Petterson said in a telephone interview. About 200 residents were on board when the disembarkation was ordered, he said. Fuel costs for the company have risen over 300 per cent since the start of the US-Israel war on Iran, Villa Vie Residences said, making the “current operating model extremely challenging”. Per-cabin fuel costs, which have historically averaged about $US1800 ($2557) a month, surged to $US6000 to $US8000, it said.

Advertisement

Passengers baulked at a request to chip in to help cover the cost of fuel to depart Cambodia, Petterson said. The company is now proposing that passengers pay roughly $US500 more a month, in addition to a fuel surcharge, as long as prices remain elevated, he said. The company is also seeking financing to depart the area “quite quickly”, Petterson added. Odyssey has been at sea since October 2024, and it’s not like a typical cruise line. Its passengers either rent, own or rent-to-own cabins on the ship. According to a brochure, cabin prices for permanent residency range from just under $US130,000 to $US440,000 for a suite, with monthly fees of $US2000 to $US10,000. Related Article Cruises Nearly 2km long, 80,000 passengers: The wild plan for a floating city The vessel departed Belfast, Ireland, for a “continuous” voyage around the world, according to the company’s website. It’s unclear where stranded passengers and staff will go after disembarking in Cambodia. The company press release said it “recognises that this is a difficult and disruptive period for residents, crew members, and employees”. Fuel costs have lifted monthly operating costs by about 50 per cent to $US3 million, Petterson said.

Advertisement

“When the war broke out, nobody expected that war to carry on,” he said. “Everyone saw what happened in Venezuela; it was a hit and run ... if you asked anyone, they expected fuel to be elevated for a month, a few months. When the ceasefire came, that was expected to be the end of it. Now, if you look at what the analytics say, we don’t see the end of this until Trump is out of power.” Travel costs – whether by plane, car or ship – have surged since the Iran conflict spiked the price of oil and the products made from it, including diesel, petrol and jet fuel. Those elevated costs are hitting companies’ bottom lines, feeding into inflation and rippling through the global economy. Passengers could sign up for a permanent berth on the Odyssey for a cool $US130,000. Sam Walker intends to fulfil the final year of his Roosters deal next season despite the spectacular fallout from the unravelling of his contract negotiations. Contract extension negotiations broke down on Monday when the Roosters pulled their three-year $4.2m extension offer. Club chairman Nick Politis was so incensed that the Walker camp asked for more time – he had been offered $1.2 million per season with a ratchet clause – that it was unclear whether the relationship was still tenable. Loading If the salary cap increased by 25 per cent – which is what most clubs are budgeting for – that would have taken Walker’s wage to $1.5 million. Paying any more than that was not an option for the Roosters, who privately feel the Maroons and Kangaroos playmaker wasn’t in their top-four players this year. Sources not authorised to speak publicly believe Walker sat behind superstars James Tedesco, Mark Nawaqanitawase, Robert Toia and Naufahu Whyte in the club’s talent pecking order.

Advertisement

Despite that sentiment, the Roosters’ offer to Walker – before it was rescinded – would have outstripped what any of the quartet can earn. The Roosters also feel that while Walker justified his million-dollar wage this year, steering them to a premiership behind a stacked forward pack, he still isn’t in the top echelon of NRL players. Roosters half Sam Walker’s future is uncertain. Getty Images Walker, who is in camp with Australia for the World Cup, hasn’t spoken to coach Trent Robinson since his offer was pulled. Given the ill feeling on both sides, it’s highly unlikely the parties will get back to the negotiating table. However, Walker has told those close to him that he intends to report to pre-season training once his Kangaroos commitments and mandated holiday period is completed.

Advertisement

While the Roosters are prepared to move on immediately with a halves pairing of Hugo Savala and Toby Rodwell – although speculation persists that a player swap with Cowboys star Tom Dearden could eventuate – there is still a possibility that Walker could be at Bondi in 2027 if he doesn’t find a new home. Dearden hasn’t asked for a release from North Queensland, but he has long been linked to a move to Sydney that would suit his partner, who has just given birth to a girl. While Walker’s situation has piqued the interests of rivals, none of them can afford 24-year-old without moving on players. South Sydney coach Wayne Bennett has said there’s no space for Walker in 2027, while the Broncos – who let the Maroons playmaker slip through when he was a junior – are also close to their salary cap limit. While it’s been suggested Melbourne could target Walker if they lose Cameron Munster, the Storm is still hopeful of retaining their pivot. Perth is armed with a 20 per cent marquee salary cap allowance, and are the beneficiaries of a new rule that says the Bears can have first crack at any player who doesn’t fulfil his contract. However, the incoming franchise still has four roster spots that need to be filled, meaning they couldn’t accommodate Walker unless he is heavily subsidised. The Bears have opened negotiations with Matt Burton’s management in a bid to reunite him with former Bulldogs halves partner Toby Sexton.

Kurtley Beale has been recalled to the Wallabies for the first time in five years after the 37-year-old was selected as a shock replacement for Hunter Paisami in Australia’s spring tour squad. The improbable return of Beale, who last played for the Wallabies on the spring tour in 2021, came as his new Western Force teammate James Ramm also earned a call-up to the Wallabies squad for their four-Test tour of the UK in November. Loading The news of Beale’s recall to the Wallabies came hours after it was revealed the veteran had extended his contract with the Western Force, but only on a very modest, train-and-trial deal for the 2027 season. Paisami was named in the spring tour squad last week but has since informed Wallabies coach Les Kiss he would be withdrawing due to personal reasons, having just moved to Japan with his wife and children to start with the Shizuoka Blue Revs.

Advertisement

Beale, who debuted for the Wallabies in 2009 and has played 95 Tests, will fly from Perth to meet the Wallabies in London next week. Australia’s main squad has gathered in Sydney and departs on Saturday. It’s a remarkable return for Beale, who sat out the 2023 season after being charged with sexual assault. But after being acquitted in early 2024, he returned to rugby with the Force and was even named in Joe Schmidt’s first Wallabies squad. Kurtley Beale playing for the Western Force early this month in the Super Rugby AUS competition. Getty Images However, an Achilles tendon injury suffered playing club rugby scuttled that chance of a Test comeback, but Beale returned again for the Force and has played solidly for the last two years. He was under consideration for the Australia A tour of the US but did not go due to visa issues. If Beale gets another Test cap, he will become the third-oldest Wallaby since World War II, behind Greg Holmes and Tony Miller, who played at the same age of 38 years and 113 days.

Advertisement

Ramm has been called into the Wallabies squad after the 28-year-old signed for the Force earlier this year, following four seasons of strong form for Northampton in the English Premiership. The speedy outside back – who plays both fullback and wing – has been playing for Northland in the New Zealand NPC competition for the last few months, and has been called in to bolster the Wallabies’ back three options. New Wallabies squad member James Ramm playing for Northampton. Getty Images It is not Ramm’s first time in a Wallabies squad, given the former Waratah was picked by Dave Rennie in 2020. He didn’t get a run, and after some injury issues, Ramm then departed Australia to join the Saints at the end of 2022. Ramm’s call-up comes ahead of Dylan Pietsch and Corey Toole, who were both regular starters for the Wallabies last year under Schmidt but have fallen out of favour with Kiss.

Advertisement

“With Hunter’s unavailability we’re excited by what Kurtley can bring to the group,” Kiss said. “He’s got 95 caps worth of Test experience and whilst he will primarily cover inside centre he has the versatility to play a number of positions across the backline. “Kurtley’s also been in great form for the Western Force in Super Rugby Pacific and Super Rugby AUS and is excited to contribute to the environment. Kurtley Beale at Wallabies training in 2024, before injurying his achilles tendon. Getty Images “At the same time, James is a player we’ve kept a keen eye on for a while and his form for Northland has been exceptional in recent times. “He’s someone who knows the UK well, having spent a very successful period with Northampton, and can cover multiple positions across the backline.”

Advertisement

The Wallabies also announced Kalani Thomas will be joining the touring squad as a fourth halfback, given Tate McDermott is on standby to return to Australia for the birth of his first child. Thomas, who is with the Australia A squad in the USA, will join Ryan Lonergan, Teddy Wilson and McDermott. Related Article Australian rugby Wallabies sweat on Hooper availability after star forward aggravates shoulder injury Meanwhile, fears about Tom Hooper being ruled out of action for the entire four-Test tour have been allayed, with positive news emerging from scans on an injured shoulder. Hooper left the field in a game for Exeter at the weekend after copping a knock on the same shoulder in which he suffered a fractured scapula in early July, when playing for the Wallabies against Ireland. There were concerns Hooper could miss all the Wallabies’ matches in November if there was a re-fracture, but scans have ruled that out, according to informed sources. While Hooper may miss the opening Test against England on November 9, there are now hopes the big back-rower will be fit to take on Scotland and Wales in the following weeks.

Olympic great Ariarne Titmus has revealed she was subjected to thousands of hateful messages after criticising a provocative Sydney Sweeney advertisement, saying she was personally attacked over her appearance for standing up for women’s sport. Last month, Titmus joined a chorus of prominent female athletes condemning an advertisement featuring American actress Sydney Sweeney, who appeared scantily clad alongside various pieces of sporting equipment. Sydney Sweeney poses for her controversial Novig ad, which Olympian Ariarne Titmus has criticised. The advertisement, filmed for US sports prediction platform Novig, played on the company’s “just sports” slogan. The former Australian swimmer described it as “an absolute joke” and “the furthest thing from sport”.

Advertisement

“I can’t describe how infuriated I feel when I watch this,” Titmus wrote on social media. “Not only is it a kick in the face to every woman who has dedicated her life to perfecting her craft, but every woman who enjoys sports for what it really is.” Ariarne Titmus’ Instagram response to the Sydney Sweeney advertising campaign. Instagram Titmus received support from fellow Olympians and other prominent female athletes, many of whom shared their own criticism of the advertisement. Speaking at a Racing NSW media event ahead of Golden Eagle Day at Royal Randwick on Saturday, Titmus said she had no idea her comments, posted while holidaying in Europe, would generate such a fierce reaction.

“I got a lot of messages of support but at the same time, I got thousands of comments and messages of hate. It’s unfortunate,” Titmus told this masthead on Wednesday. “I was just trying to do the right thing and use my platform. Being removed from the swimming team now, I feel I can be a bit more vocal … but I was quite surprised by the reception. “But you know what? I’d do it again. I just think how far we come and how incredible our female athletes are around the world. It didn’t sit very nicely with me. Ariarne Titmus at Royal Randwick Racecourse on Wednesday ahead of Saturday’s Golden Eagle Day. Sitthixay Ditthavong “I was quite lucky throughout my swimming career. I never really got much trolling or hate, and I always felt immense support. It was the first time I felt people were attacking me personally and physically [about] how I looked.” Did it affect her?

“It kind of just goes over my head,” she said. “I know who I am. That’s their problem. A lot of them were probably bots, to be honest. Other women who spoke out about it probably got the same [treatment].” It has been just over a year since Titmus, an eight-time Olympic medallist, world record holder and world champion, announced her retirement from swimming. Ariarne Titmus after winning gold in the 400m freestyle at the 2024 Olympic Games. AP Training to become the best swimmer in the world was taxing, but retirement has hardly meant putting her feet up. The past 12 months have been a whirlwind of flights, sponsor appearances and broadcast commitments as Titmus establishes herself beyond the pool. Titmus, who is launching her book Relentless next week, has also partnered with Youngcare to raise awareness of the charity’s work helping young Australians with complex and permanent physical disabilities live independently.

Advertisement

Golden Eagle Day has become one of Australia’s biggest race days, with about $1 million donated to charities each year. For Titmus, the association with racing is fitting. Long before she became a swimming superstar, horses were her first love. She grew up riding them on her family’s property in Tasmania before committing to the pool. Ariarne Titmus with inaugural Golden Eagle winner Kolding at Royal Randwick. Sitthixay Ditthavong With the 2028 Los Angeles Olympics less than two years away, Titmus insists there is no temptation to make a comeback. “The chapter is well and truly closed,” Titmus said. “Zero part of me wanted to be in the water [at the recent Commonwealth Games in Glasgow]. I felt so removed from that team. Every day that’s passed since I’ve retired, I know that it’s the right one.

“I haven’t slowed down. I really thought that it might have a bit of a lull, but I’ve just thrown myself into as much as I possibly can, and the work’s been coming.” Titmus is also preparing for the release of her autobiography on Tuesday, which promises a warts-and-all account of her extraordinary career and the demanding methods of longtime coach Dean Boxall. Their partnership delivered Olympic gold medals and world records, but although it was not always smooth sailing, there was always mutual respect. “I don’t regret one second of it or how hard I pushed myself. It’s definitely a feel-good story,” Titmus said.

“We had big blow-ups. He used to call me a ‘self-cleaning carpet’ because we’d have a big blow-up and then I come back the next day like nothing happened. “In the hard times or the blow-ups – and in the moments where he was pushing me to the brink – I really made sure it was well known that that’s what I wanted from him. I knew that I thrive with that bad cop on my back.”

The Coalition’s proposal to convert Long Bay jail into 12,000 homes has erupted into a fight over the future of housing in prime Sydney locations, with Planning Minister Paul Scully labelling it a fantasy. As Opposition Leader Kellie Sloane questioned why a prison occupied 50 hectares of prime real estate in Sydney’s eastern suburbs, Scully decried the plan as “nothing more than a multibillion-dollar bill to the taxpayer masquerading as a housing plan”. (From left) Maroubra MP and Attorney-General Michael Daley, Planning Minister Paul Scully, and Corrections Minister Anoulack Chanthivong outside Long Bay jail on Wednesday. Sitthixay Ditthavong The housing battle has turned personal after the Coalition and Labor each released plans for massive redevelopments in safe seats held by the opposing party: Woollahra and Edgecliff in Sloane’s seat of Vaucluse, and the Long Bay plan in Attorney-General Michael Daley’s seat of Maroubra. Hours after this masthead revealed the Liberals’ plan to establish a delivery authority to organise the closure of Long Bay prison within 100 days if elected in March, three Labor ministers stood outside the corrections centre on Wednesday to condemn the proposal as unworkable.

Advertisement

“What we’ve seen from the member for Vaucluse and the Liberal Party is a plan to not have housing in Woollahra. This is a distraction and a fantasy of an idea,” Scully said. “The reality is the idea of putting 12,000 homes on the site behind us would create an area of around three times the density of Green Square without any of the transport infrastructure. This doesn’t pass the most basic of planning tests.” The jail houses about 1200 inmates, but the Liberals say there is space for about 12,000 dwellings. Sitthixay Ditthavong Daley said the proposed uplift in density was unworkable given Anzac Parade – the only road in or out of the peninsula – was already “chock-a-block” in the morning. Premier Chris Minns has previously said the only way to make the redevelopment stack up is by building a metro station nearby, which the government has no plans to do. Scully said there were several unanswered questions about the Coalition proposal, including where the jail’s 1200 inmates would be rehoused, and the overall cost. Sloane has suggested selling the land to developers could yield the government up to $2 billion.

Advertisement

Opposition planning spokesman Chris Rath accused the government of claiming they were pro-housing while rejecting each of the Coalition’s three planning proposals, including building 10,000 new homes in the inner west and 10,000 new homes in Camellia-Rosehill. Related Article Exclusive

NSW State Parliament NSW Liberals abandon YIMBY truce as housing goes on the ballot “So they talk a big game on housing, but when it comes to actually delivering, they are 40 per cent behind their National Housing Accord target. And it’s very disappointing today to see that they’re against our plan for 12,000 new homes right here at Long Bay,” he said. In an interview with ABC Sydney on Wednesday morning, Sloane was unable to say what the proposed cost of the redevelopment would be, nor where Long Bay’s 1200 inmates would be rehoused if the proposal went ahead. She argued a delivery authority would be established to work through those issues. Sloane acknowledged the plan would require upgraded transport infrastructure “down the track”, suggesting the extension of the light rail down Anzac Parade was an idea. Cricket Australia chief executive Todd Greenberg has revealed he is in “deep conversations” with national selectors about regenerating an ageing Test team, as it emerged contract discussions with coach Andrew McDonald had also opened. Speaking after Wednesday’s CA annual general meeting, where the organisation revealed it had taken a combined $20 million hit because of a pair of two-day Ashes Tests last summer, Greenberg said he was aware selection chairman George Bailey and his panel had tough decisions to make. Coach Andrew McDonald and chairman of selectors George Bailey will need to usher new players in to the Test team. ICC via Getty Images The futures of Steve Smith, 37, Nathan Lyon, 38, Scott Boland, 37, Mitchell Starc, 36, Josh Hazlewood, 35, and skipper Pat Cummins, 33, who have been central to a largely winning era, are up for debate, while Marnus Labuschagne, 32, is fighting for his Test future in the ongoing third and final Test against South Africa in Cape Town. Greenberg has just returned from South Africa, where selection, particularly heading into Newlands, had been contentious, with three players dropped, and Smith out because of injury.

“Yes, we are in deep conversations about how this team will look and operate over the next six, 12, 18, 24 months,” Greenberg said. Related Article Analysis

But we have an eye on what that looks like after they finish their playing days. We don’t know when that will be but, of course, we’ve got to have an eye on what the transition looks like.” After a home Test summer against New Zealand, Australia have heavy-duty tours of India and England to negotiate. McDonald, who boasts a fantastic record since replacing Justin Langer in 2022, is contracted until the end of next year’s World Cup in South Africa. An industry source, not authorised to speak publicly, said McDonald’s focus was on the current tour, but he was “open” to coaching on. He’s held in incredibly high regard by the Cricket Australia board and by all of us,” Greenberg said. “I think he’s done an outstanding job, and I think his results tell you that. But in saying that, there’s also an eye of what’s coming next, and there’s, no doubt, that there’ll be a transition of this team, and we want to make sure that we can have oversight of that so that we protect and thrive into the next phase, whoever that might be.” Mike Baird resigned from his role at Cricket Australia last month, but still insists BBL privatisation is the best way forward. Getty Outgoing chairman Mike Baird presided over his final AGM, having last month lost the support of his home state, Cricket NSW, to carry on as a director, amid ructions over plans to privatise BBL clubs. However, David Boon, who assumed the role of interim chair on Wednesday following Baird’s official departure, declared the sport’s governing body would plough on with the contentious plans that have attracted interest from up to 30 Indian, European and US-based entities, who have had access to a data room.

Cricket Victoria is pushing to sell-off 100 per cent of the Melbourne Renegades by the end of this year, while Greenberg said Tasmania, through the Hobart Hurricanes, and Western Australia, through the Perth Scorchers, were “actively engaged” in the “self-determination” model suggested by South Australia. Mitchell Starc’s devastating burst on the shadow of stumps not only saved his captain but also his team. A day in which Australia were behind from the moment Pat Cummins sent South Africa in to bat finished with honours shared after Starc’s match-turning four wickets in the space of six deliveries. Mitchell Starc rescued Australia on Tuesday in Cape Town. AP Photo/Halden Krog Only those in the camp can honestly answer if the visitors would have settled for a Proteas total of 329 if offered before the day, but such a scoreline would have been gleefully accepted when openers Aiden Markram and Marques Ackerman destroyed the new ball. So dominant were they in reaching 0-158, Cummins’ decision to bowl first was rivalling that of former England captain Nasser Hussain, whose infamous call to send Australia in at the Gabba in 2002 resulted in a stumps score of 2-364.

The hosts were still in control when Cummins handed Starc a second brand-new Kookaburra about 20 minutes before stumps. Related Article Updated

Australian cricket Cricket Australia boss has ‘deep conversations’ with selectors about Test team At 6-325, a score of 400-plus was on the cards for the Proteas, who had wicketkeeper Ryan Rickelton and damaging all-rounder Marco Jansen settled at the crease and another of their lower-order tormentors from Gqeberha, Simon Harmer, padded up in the pavilion. Hours earlier in the first session, Starc – and Australia’s vaunted quicks – repeatedly found the middle of the bat. Now, his golden left arm was launching missiles that curved wickedly late to smash pads and stumps. Starc, who had seen Travis Head drop a dolly, did not need his teammates. His final four victims were all out bowled or lbw.

Shortly after tea, Starc had the unflattering figures of 0-62 from 12 overs. By the close of play, he had taken his 20th bag of five or more wickets, his analysis of 6-72 his seventh-best return in his 110-Test career. Of his eight best figures, six have come in his past two years. Age is not wearying him. 80.4 overs, Ryan Rickelton lbw b Starc 42 (South Africa: 7-327) After capturing his first two wickets with bouncers on a surface not offering much lateral movement off the seam, Starc made the pitch just about a non-factor. Armed with the second new ball, Starc aimed full and straight to Rickelton, who had provided the ballast in an ominous 95-run stand with the damaging Jansen.

Advertisement

The yorker straightened and swung extremely late, thudding into the back pad of Rickelton, who had been squared up by a delivery he attempted to play through mid-wicket when a fuller face of the bat was needed. A despondent, and defeated, Rickelton accepted his fate without asking the video umpire for salvation. 80.6 overs, Marco Jansen b Starc 52 (South Africa: 8-328) Jansen was the pick of Starc’s wickets, dismissed by a 143.6 km/h thunderbolt that was reminiscent of his delivery to New Zealand great Brendon McCullum in the 2015 World Cup final.

Having spent the best part of two hours at the crease for his 52, Jansen’s eye was well and truly in, but he was beaten for pace and swing. He played late and down the wrong line, unable to jam his bat down on a ball to prevent it from clattering into the base of his off stump. 82.1 overs, Gerald Coetzee b Starc 0 (South Africa 9-329) With a Test average of 13.40, Gerald Coetzee is no bunny with the bat, so it’s understandable why his partner Simon Harmer did not attempt to shield the No.10 from Starc. He should have. The man who made a career-best 82 last week did not face another ball.

After seeing his more skilled teammates fired out by Starc’s yorkers, Coetzee did not want his toes near the ball first up. He backed away slightly to a 144.1 km/h full delivery, which ricocheted off his front pad into the stumps for a golden globe. 82.3 Kagiso Rabada lbw b Starc 0 (South Africa 329 all out) There was no disgrace in Kagiso Rabada’s dismissal, trapped plumb in front to almost the identical delivery that removed Rickelton minutes earlier. If a top-six batter with a Test average of nearly 50 could not defend it, then what hope for a No.11?

‘Completion gives us a clear run at construction and commissioning, with feedstock contracted.’ Hastings Technology Metals chief executive officer Vince Catania Hastings says testing and commissioning are on track to kick off in the first quarter, with first production expected to follow shortly after. Importantly, the company says it has de-risked the plant’s start-up phase by securing a binding feedstock supply agreement with Enuo for a minimum of 10,000 tonnes per annum of monazite concentrate. The supply is expected to come from Africa, giving Hastings an independent source of feed while its flagship Yangibana project in Western Australia is brought online to potentially provide a longer-term runway for the plant’s initial years of operation. Hastings Technology Metals chief executive officer Vince Catania said: “Completion gives us a clear run at construction and commissioning, with feedstock contracted. The plant chemically cracks and leaches monazite concentrate into mixed rare earth chloride (MREC), an intermediate product for specialist rare earths separation plants.

It could also provide significant tax incentives, including a corporate income tax exemption for up to 13 years. By picking up a near-term production asset in Thailand, Hastings has found a shortcut to cash flow and skipped the long lead times that stall so many aspiring miners. Richard Tognetti, the artistic director and lead violin of the Australian Chamber Orchestra, seems remarkably chill for someone who’s “working frantically”, as he puts it. Currently wrapping up the ACO’s 50th anniversary with a national tour of Beethoven’s Pastoral (aka Symphony No. 6), his mind’s already deep in the orchestra’s program for 2027, which will be led by Johann Sebastian Bach’s St John Passion. “It’s simply one of the greatest works ever conceived by humankind,” says Tognetti from his beachside home in Manly. “J.S. Bach is widely believed by anyone who cares to know about such things these days as the greatest composer, and his two surviving passions – the St Matthew and St John – are regarded as these extraordinary musical events. It’s going to be a pretty good year.” Richard Tognetti, the Australian Chamber Orchestra’s artistic director and lead violin, regrets the stupidity of our politicians. Georges Antoni Worst habit? Impatience. I’ve always got 15 plates in the air and way too many projects, so I’m always lying awake at night, worrying about things I need to get done. As technology gets faster, our impatience gets worse, which is ridiculous. So recently, I set myself up with a turntable hi-fi system. It’s vinyl-only, and you’re only allowed to use it if you listen to a whole side of a record.

Advertisement

Greatest fear? The shark problem. Surfing is my life. I grew up in Wollongong, and I’ve been surfing since I was a kid. So, as a surfer, my greatest fear is that the shark problem is going to become so unmanageable that we’ll become a Reunion Island “paradise” with no swimming or surfing. Unfortunately, it’s become a highly politicised issue. The trolling on the internet is almost a joke. It’s people who don’t even know what the ocean is saying, “Well, you deserve to die because you’re in their backyard.” There’s a lot of misinformation and emotional anxiety, and what we’re left with is a lot of fear and distress in the surfing and ocean swimming community. The line that has stayed with you? “Art makes grand our own stupid lives.” Seven dangerous words. I think I got it from Clive James’ amazing book, Cultural Amnesia. It’s self-explanatory but it means that art – which is everywhere – elevates you in a way that makes you feel the world is more interesting than it actually is.

Advertisement

The more we can be involved in cultural pursuits, the better off we are. At the least, it keeps us out of trouble. If a kid plays a clarinet and they’re obsessed with playing it well, it focuses the brain, you get emotional expression, it brings joy to people. Art does that. It’s interesting that there’s a lot of talk about saving Western culture these days, but most of the people who make us paranoid about it are those who don’t even consider its merits. I wish politicians would read more. I was involved in a rather narky incident with a very well-known politician who told me they don’t have time to read, and I just thought, “Therein lies the problem.” Tognetti began playing violin at the age of five: “It takes years just to get a reasonable sound,” he says. Georges Antoni Biggest regret? I think it was Helen Mirren who was once asked this and she said, “I didn’t tell enough people to f--- off.” [laughs] Well, we all know what she means. But I suppose my biggest regret at my age is that I’ve tried so hard to convince politicians about the value of music education and to this day, I regret that more of them haven’t listened. It’s shithouse, totally depressing, and if anything they’re making it worse.

Advertisement

It’s a no-brainer, learning how to read and write and appreciate music. And not just Mozart, but lots of different types of music. Have you ever met someone who said, “I learned to play the guitar when I was young and I really regret it”? No! So I regret I couldn’t convince these people. I take full responsibility for the stupidity of politicians. Tell us about your turning point. When you start playing piano as a kid, if you just work at it a bit, with one note you can make as good a sound as any pianist who’s ever lived. With a violin, no way! It takes years just to get a reasonable sound. I think it was in 1974 in Wollongong. I would’ve been about eight. I remember standing on a stage and playing my own little pathetic piece and just thinking, “Wow, I can actually kind of play.” That was a turning point. I started playing violin when I was five. The worst thing I hear is parents saying about their kids, “Oh my God, it sounds like shit.” Yeah, we know it sounds like shit… until it doesn’t!

Advertisement

What is the song you wish was yours? The last movement of Symphony No. 41 by Wolfgang Amadeus Mozart, which is nicknamed the “Jupiter Symphony” for good reason. As incredible as Bach is, and possibly we could all agree that he’s the greatest composer, here is Mozart bringing together tunes from the street, opera tunes, ecclesiastical melodies and balancing, like, seven of them at one time so that all you’ve got is pure exhilaration. That for me is, wow. If I wrote that, I’d be like, yep, that’ll do. And then the poor bastard goes and dies at 35! It was one of the last things he wrote. If you could time travel, where would you choose to go? The fairly sophisticated times of Mozart’s Vienna. Which is nothing like modern-day Vienna. As much as the modern-day Viennese musicians will have you believe they’re connected to Mozart, they’re not in any way or form.

title: The billion-dollar cancer bill Australia's sunscreen overhaul may not fix
text:
in brief The regulator is now developing reforms to strengthen sunscreen testing.

But experts say more reliable testing is only part of the solution.

Australia's sunscreen regulator is planning tougher rules after concerns some products failed to deliver the sun protection promised on their labels.

But experts say more reliable testing is only part of the solution, with boosting awareness on how Australians need to apply and reapply sunscreen also critical to preventing skin cancer.

In a report published last year, consumer group CHOICE tested 20 popular sunscreens and found that only four met their labelled sun protection factor (SPF), raising questions about the reliability of products Australians rely on to protect themselves from UV radiation.

The Therapeutic Goods Administration (TGA) later recalled several sunscreen products after identifying batches that didn't deliver their advertised SPF protection.

The regulator is now developing reforms to strengthen sunscreen testing, improve ingredient-quality requirements, and clarify the SPF claims cosmetic products can make.

Enter email address Subscribe Morning (Mon–Fri) Afternoon (Mon–Fri) Weekend Insight By subscribing, you agree to SBS’s terms of service and privacy policy including receiving email updates from SBS.

What are the proposed reforms?

The TGA is proposing several reforms to address sunscreen quality, with the goal of reducing instances of skin cancer.

Australia has the highest rate of melanoma incidence in the world, with an estimated 17,443 new cases diagnosed in 2025 according to Cancer Australia.

The reforms are:

Strengthen sunscreen testing requirements

Develop specific ingredient quality requirements

Provide a consistent limit for SPF rating that can be claimed for all secondary (cosmetic) sunscreens

Review sunscreen good manufacturing practice guidance

Consider labelling for SPF ratings

Professor Terry Slevin, CEO of the Public Health Association of Australia, told SBS News that treating skin cancers costs the country more than $1 billion each year.

"We need to invest more in preventing those cancers rather than having to treat them at the tail end," he said.

The TGA told SBS News: "The proposed reforms are intended to provide greater assurance through stronger testing requirements, increased oversight of testing laboratories, testing of finished products and periodic testing over a product’s lifecycle, and improved access by the TGA to SPF testing evidence."

Improving testing

Improving how sunscreen is tested is one way the TGA wants to improve quality and reliability of SPF claims.

Slevin explained that a small number of labs in Australia produce the nation's sunscreen, supplying multiple brands.

Sunscreens can then be tested on volunteers who use the formula and are then exposed to UV radiation; the rate at which skin reddens can then be used to determine the product's quality.

Experts say sunscreen safety is not just about the products, but also how we apply it. Source: AAP / Dan Himbrechts

While this method is common, it can also be imprecise.

"People have different skin types, and the amount of product being applied can vary a lot. So having consistent SPF levels relies on a lot of unpredictable variables," Slevin said.

These variations can lead to inconsistent product application and to sunscreens having marginally different SPF than advertised on their packaging.

Should you be worried about SPF levels?

The TGA reforms are looking to ensure that sunscreen manufacturers have clearer guidance and expectations, but SPF levels could still slightly vary from bottle to bottle according to Slevin.

However, variations would be minimal and would have little impact on the sunscreen's efficacy.

"The difference between SPF 50 and SPF 30 may sound significant, but the difference in the amount of UV that’s filtered out is only 3 per cent, a small change," he said.

"The vast majority of sunscreens serve a very useful and effective purpose; these reforms will only strengthen this."

But the main way to achieve the TGA's goal may not be reforming testing, but educating people on how to use sunscreen products best.

Dispelling confusion

Anna Wang, an associate professor in the School of Chemistry at UNSW Sydney, said that improving consumer understanding and behaviour is the best way to improve sun safety.

"What is going to make a bigger impact isn’t whether a sunscreen tests SPF45 using one method and SPF40 using another, but how often we reapply, and whether we put the recommended amount on," she told SBS News.

Experts recommended applying sunscreen generously to all exposed skin every two hours, seeking shade, and wearing a hat and sunglasses.

Towelling off after a swim, or wiping water or sweat off your body, can also remove some sunscreen.

Some cosmetic products, including foundations and moisturisers, also advertise SPF protection.

The TGA is considering a consistent limit on the SPF ratings these secondary sunscreens can claim, aiming to make it easier for consumers to distinguish products designed primarily for sun protection from those intended mainly for cosmetic use.

"In Australia, we have several hundred formulations to choose from so it can be confusing," Wang said.

She supported the TGA's reforms to clarify the distinction between primary and secondary sunscreens.

Investigation ongoing

In the meantime, the TGA confirmed to SBS News its investigation into sunscreens with disputed SPF results is ongoing.

"The TGA is considering the available evidence and providing sponsors with an opportunity to provide additional data or evidence before regulatory decisions are made," it told SBS News.

The regulator said it will issue product recalls or cancellations as needed while it develops the new reforms.

"The TGA intends to publish its findings and learnings and provide further guidance to sponsors and manufacturers to clarify expectations around SPF evidence and testing."

title: Inflation 'persisting longer' than desired, Treasurer says, after surprising spike
text:
In brief Core inflation rose faster than expected, adding to pressure on the Reserve Bank.

Fresh inflation data has fuelled expectations of another interest rate hike.

Core inflation climbed 1 per cent in Australia over the quarter, with the Reserve Bank governor warning underlying inflation is still too high.

The September quarter increase in the trimmed mean was in line with economists' expectations but exceeded the central bank's forecast of a 0.8 per cent increase.

On an annualised basis, the trimmed mean — a measure of underlying inflation that removes the biggest price swings — rose 3.6 per cent.

Headline inflation was hotter than expected by the market, at 1.3 per cent over the quarter.

Treasurer Jim Chalmers acknowledged inflation is persisting "longer than anyone would like" and citing the war in the Middle East as a major factor.

Markets had upped their bets for a November hike after comments in the past week by the Reserve Bank of Australia's (RBA) deputy governor, Andrew Hauser, and chief economist Sarah Hunter, indicating that inflation remained too high.

At the same time as the data was published by the Australian Bureau of Statistics, RBA governor Michele Bullock was appearing alongside Hauser, Hunter and other top officials at a Senate estimates hearing.

Elevated underlying inflationary pressures were a sign that the labour market was still tight, Bullock said.

"The Monetary Policy Board will meet next week," she said.

"We'll discuss our assessment of the flow of data and how the risks are unfolding. A key question is whether the tightening in monetary policy to date will be sufficient to bring inflation back to target in a reasonable time."

Monthly headline inflation rose 4.3 per cent on an annual basis, up from 4 per cent in the 12 months to August.

"Housing was the largest contributor to annual inflation in September, rising by 5.2 per cent," said Rachael McCririck, ABS head of price statistics.

Transport was the second largest contributor, rising by 8.7 per cent annually, due to higher fuel costs.

Fuel and the war in the Middle East

Speaking to press in Canberra, Treasurer Jim Chalmers issued a small mea culpa.

"We accept our part in the fight against inflation," Chalmers said.

"We take responsibility for government policy when it comes to the fiscal settings and when it comes to managing the budget in a responsible way in the face of this inflation challenge, which is persisting longer than anyone would like."

Chalmers again blamed rising inflation on higher fuel prices driven by the conflict in the Middle East.

"This war in the Middle East has been disastrous for Australians, for cost of living, and for inflation right around the world," he said.

"The point that [Treasury] secretary [Jenny] Wilkinson made today and the point that governor Bullock made today is that global energy prices are much higher than have been assumed. And we know what's driving that."

Speaking to reporters after Chalmers' conference, Opposition treasury spokesperson Tim Wilson said Australian families need the government to get inflation under control.

"There will be a lot of households, family, sitting around the kitchen tables of the nation figuring out — what is left to cut? Small business owners who will take this inflation data as a kick directly at their future opportunity and their hope."

title: 'The fire is out': Star casino's future in doubt after huge money laundering fine

The penalty leaves Australia's biggest listed casino operator facing an uncertain future.

Australia's biggest listed casino company is on the brink of administration after being fined $260 million for historical money-laundering violations.

The Star Entertainment Group was fined in the Federal Court on Wednesday, four years after financial intelligence agency AUSTRAC launched legal action against the company.

The agency previously argued a $400 million penalty was necessary to punish what it said were "manifest failures" at Star.

title: The $9 billion fuel bill raising questions about Australia's energy security
text:
In brief Australia paid a higher price for imported diesel than any other nation during the fuel crisis.

New analysis linked billions in extra fuel costs to energy security risks.

Australia has paid more than twice as much as any other nation in additional diesel import costs during the global fuel crisis, with a report putting the toll at $9 billion over six months.

The added cost equates to $324 for every Australian, exceeding the bills incurred by Brazil, South Africa, France and the UK.

The Climate Council released the figures from its energy security scorecard on Wednesday, which also found Australia paid an extra $1.6 billion for petrol imports.

The findings come days after oil prices reached a six-month high amid escalating threats in the Middle East.

The council's report, called Crude Awakening, analysed Australia's energy security, its exposure to rising global fuel prices, and policies and progress towards electric transport and renewable energy.

Enter email address Subscribe Morning (Mon–Fri) Afternoon (Mon–Fri) Weekend Insight By subscribing, you agree to SBS’s terms of service and privacy policy including receiving email updates from SBS.

It found Australia was the world's largest seaborne importer of diesel, with imports responsible for 90 per cent of its supply.

Diesel use in Australia had also more than doubled since 2000 to 33 billion litres in 2025, with about a quarter used in mining.

Australia paid $9 billion in additional costs to import diesel between March and August, compared to an extra $3.5 billion in Brazil and $3 billion in the UK.

The nation also paid an additional $1.6 billion for petrol, or $56 per person.

READ MORE Australians are becoming less convinced about what comes next

Climate Council spokeswoman and economist Nicki Hutley said those costs had a widespread impact.

"We're seeing costs (rise) right through the economy, whether it's in inflation at the supermarket or all the way through the supply chain," she told the Australian Associated Press news agency.

"If we keep relying on imported oil, that is leaving our energy security in somebody else's hands, and we're seeing that this year."

Moves to renewable energy had saved Australians from some higher costs, the report found, with electric and hybrid cars cutting $1.7 billion in costs and saving the equivalent of 17.4 million litres of petrol and diesel per week.

Australia was still slow to adopt electric trucks, with the vehicles representing 0.7 per cent of new sales compared to nine per cent worldwide, and had one public charging point for every 41 electric cars, compared to the global average of one for every 11 EVs.

Electrifying more vehicles and removing diesel fuel tax credits could help to protect Australia from future fuel shocks, Hutley said, and state and federal policies should support the transition.

title: More Australians are seeing a GP. What happens next is becoming more complex
text:
IN BRIEF Australian doctors are bridging gaps in the medical system as mental health presentations increase.

Longer consultation times are being driven by "increasingly complex" patient needs.

General practitioners (GPs) are spending more time with patients, treating increasingly complex conditions and working across specialist remits, according to a new report.

The Royal Australian College of GPs (RACGP) is calling on the federal government to increase Medicare patient rebates for longer consultations, after its latest Health of the Nation report found that two-thirds of GPs were spending more time with patients than in previous years.

In 2026, the average consultation length increased to 19.8 minutes per patient, up from 19.7 minutes in 2025 and 17.7 minutes in 2022.

Over 70 per cent of the 2,766 Australian GPs surveyed in the report identified increasingly complex care as their biggest issue — driven by growing rates of chronic disease, high rates of mental health presentations and an ageing population.

Psychological presentations were the leading reason patients sought care in 2025, reported by 67 per cent of practising GPs.

The figure has remained high over the past decade, rising from 61 per cent in 2017 to a high of 72 per cent in 2023 following the COVID-19 pandemic.

One GP quoted in the study said there had been a "marked rise" in anxiety, depression, trauma-related disorders and social isolation across all age groups, especially among young adults and working-age populations.

"Many presentations are linked to financial stress, housing insecurity, workplace pressures, and relationship breakdowns rather than purely medical causes."

The range of reasons GPs are spending more time with patients is wide and varied. Source: SBS News

More patients were presenting with complex psycho-social needs, requiring longer consultations, continuity of care, and multidisciplinary support, which was "difficult to sustain within current funding models".

Head of the Health Economics Group at Monash University's School of Public Health and Preventative Medicine, Professor Cathy Mihalopoulos, told SBS News GPs respond to a range of mental health conditions.

She said they most commonly see a "breadth of severity" in "high prevalence" conditions such as anxiety and depression.

"For a lot of GPs, the commitment is to do the best they can for the person sitting in front of them ... they absolutely want to do the best they can, but the problems they're confronted with often aren't something you can easily solve in five minutes," she said.

The health economist said part of the pressure on GPs is a lack of services for the "missing middle" — patients whose needs sit between what a GP and a specialised service provides.

"These are people who are not mild, and they're not very severe .... they're in that missing middle," she said.

"Their care often falls to GPs, but their care is quite complex in terms of the things they may have to deal with."

She said GPs play a crucial role in helping those seeking support for their mental health to navigate a "fragmented" health system.

The report also found GPs were helping alleviate pressure on hospital services and bridge gaps in the healthcare system.

In 2026, almost 90 per cent of GPs managed conditions usually treated by non-GP specialists, and 76 per cent managed conditions typically treated in emergency departments or urgent care settings.

Bulk billing increases

The proportion of patients bulk billed for all GP visits rose to 63 per cent in 2026, up from 56 per cent in each of the previous two years, which the report attributed to increased Medicare incentives.

RACGP president Dr Michael Wright said increased government investment in Medicare to $489 per person in 2026 was an important recognition of general practice's role in Australian healthcare, but that more investment was needed to cover longer consultations.

"The challenge is that the Medicare system has not kept pace with the realities of modern general practice, and funding does not adequately support the time required to provide the care patients need."

Bulk billing incentives have reduced out-of-pocket costs, but some Australians are still delaying their healthcare. Source: AAP / Darren England

The rate of Australians delaying seeking healthcare due to cost fell from 8.8 per cent in 2025 to 7.7 per cent in 2026. Young adults aged 25 to 34 remain the most likely to delay care because of cost.

Mihalopoulos said it remains a "real problem".

"We should not be delaying seeking care for our health, because everything depends on our good health," she said.

She said while bulk billing incentives have contributed to increased presentations, Australia is not "100 per cent there yet".

"Getting people into care earlier and addressing their needs is crucial."

Intersectional outcomes

For the first time, women GPs reported less satisfaction with their jobs than their male counterparts, with the proportion of female GPs recommending the profession to younger colleagues dropping from 53 per cent in 2025 to 48 per cent in 2026.

In 2026, female GPs saw a higher proportion of patients presenting with complex psycho-social issues, mental health concerns and women's health matters, and spent more time with patients on average than their male counterparts.

Racism was also identified as part of some GPs' experience, with more than 30 per cent agreeing that they had witnessed racism towards patients within the broader healthcare system, and 19 per cent reporting personally experiencing racism in the past year.

While 6 per cent of GPs said they had personally experienced racism from a colleague within their practice, 65 per cent said they were confident in addressing or challenging racism from patients or colleagues within their practice and the broader healthcare system.
