title: Wells says Bluey reflects Australian values while Joyce criticises intolerance of satire
text:
IN BRIEF One Nation is under fire for its use of Bluey in a 2024 episode of the party's Please Explain series.

In the episode, it's implied that Bluey mows down Daniel Andrews and Anthony Albanese with a car.

Communications Minister Anika Wells says the ABC is "well within its rights" to be concerned about a One Nation video in which its beloved character Bluey is run over by a car.

The Australian cartoon dog appeared in a 2024 episode of One Nation's Please Explain series, now the subject of legal action by the ABC.

In the episode, a car driven by former Victorian premier Daniel Andrews hits Bluey, with Prime Minister Anthony Albanese in the passenger seat.

The episode implies the battered Bluey mows down the premier and prime minister later in the episode, titled The State of Melbourne.

"Bluey is one of Australia's biggest, most large, most well-known exports. I think the ABC's well within its rights to be concerned here," Wells told ABC RN on Wednesday morning.

Wells acknowledged the video series is satirical, but said there is a line between satirising politics and making a politician's life "unbearable".

"It's certainly not something that I would produce or that I would ever ask my team to produce," she said.

'We will be taking further action'

ABC managing director Hugh Marks said it was a "shocking use of Australia's most loved character" in a Senate estimates hearing on Tuesday.

"Probably the globally most loved character in a video that is both shocking and disrespectful to the children of Australia," he said.

"I can't substantiate it either legally, or on the basis of its usage."

Labor senator Varun Ghosh described Bluey's use as "heinous", particularly in light of the alleged attack on independent MP Helen Haines on 19 October, where she was hit by a car and lost both legs.

To Marks' knowledge, One Nation had not licensed Bluey's likeness from BBC Studios, which distributes the TV show, but could still be entitled to show the character under fair use provisions if Please Explain is considered satire or parody.

But the ABC boss said he did not think that defence would suffice.

"It's not a parody of any Bluey work, it's not a minor use of the (intellectual property). In my view, it is an infringement of the intellectual property," he said.

"I think it's a blatant use.

"We will be taking further action. I can assure you."

The broadcaster will write One Nation a cease and desist letter demanding the video be taken down, with Marks flagging it may seek damages.

The party used Bluey in another Please Explain episode about Queensland, where the dog did not drive into any politicians.

Wells declined to comment on any legal proceedings when asked, but she added: "Bluey has a lot more production value than One Nation's cartoons. We can all learn a lot from Bluey."

Joyce accuses critics of 'sanitising beyond satire'

One Nation MP Barnaby Joyce has said the Please Explain cartoons were satire and were not meant to be taken seriously.

"You get to a point where you are sanitising beyond satire and you are starting to put restrictions on us," he told ABC TV on Tuesday.

"You've got to have some form of tolerance."

Joyce has previously apologised for another One Nation cartoon calling Liberal frontbencher and former Special Air Services soldier Andrew Hastie a "traitor".

The episode remains on YouTube.

title: A missing link to Australia's newest airport comes with a $55 sting
text:
in brief Western Sydney International Airport travellers face public transport stopgaps.

The promised metro line to the airport may not be operational until mid 2028.

Western Sydney International Airport (WSI)'s opening marks Australia's first major new aviation gateway in over half a century, yet it will be a long time before visitors will be able to take a train to or from the terminal.

From its outset, state and transit authorities had promised that WSI would come complete with a high-speed, driverless metro line to connect passengers to the wider Sydney rail network.

However, disputes with contractors, corruption allegations, and deadline blowouts have left staff and travellers forced to use stop-gap methods to reach the airport, with alternative arrangements unlikely to materialise for well over a year.

In June, the NSW government was forced to concede that the delays to the metro line opening could continue until mid-2028 — some 18 months after the grand opening of WSI.

While construction delays continue, travellers and staff face limited public transport options, with private firms' alternatives costing up to $55 per person.

Temporary transport measures

While the NSW government and Sydney Metro maintained that the metro line connecting Badgerys Creek to Bradfield and St Marys would open on schedule, planning for an emergency alternative began in early 2025, internal policy documents later revealed.

After spending $11 billion on an incomplete metro line, the NSW government announced earlier this month that the WSI Link free shuttle service would ferry passengers the 20km shortfall between the terminal and St Marys railway station on the T1 Western Line.

Five suburban bus routes have also been re-routed to the airport precinct to deliver travellers to Mount Druitt, Penrith, Liverpool, Campbelltown and Leppington at standard rates.

The WSI Link shuttle bus runs every 30 minutes from 4.30am to midnight, Sunday to Thursday, and until 1am on Friday and Saturday.

Other travel options to the city

Private operator Super Shuttle WSI offers an express coach service to Parramatta, the Sydney CBD and Sydney Airport (Kingsford Smith). A single adult ticket to Parramatta costs $25 and a return $45, the single/return adult fares to the Sydney CBD are $55/$80 and for Sydney Airport they are $65/$90.

One of the primary advantages of WSI over Sydney's original Kingsford Smith Airport is its lack of curfew, allowing passengers to arrive and depart 24 hours a day. However, current public transport services keep to standard operational hours, potentially leaving some passengers and staff with limited early-morning options.

Transport for NSW defended the interim transit arrangements, stating operating hours reflect current scheduling.

"There are currently no passenger flights operating or at this moment planned between 1 and 4.30am through Western Sydney International Airport," a Transport for NSW spokesperson told SBS News. "Transport for NSW continues to monitor service demand as the airport grows."

The department said travellers arriving during the overnight window have access to private shuttles, rideshares, and vehicle parking.

While current schedules favour daytime hours, international and budget carriers are scheduled to scale up through early 2027.

Western Sydney International's limitations 'understood'

Adam Leto, CEO of the Western Sydney Leadership Dialogue, told SBS News that the airport ought to be seen in its broader context and that initial concerns over transport pale in comparison to the benefit it brings.

"Rome wasn't built in a day," Leto said. "We've understood what the airport was going to look like when it opened, and it's not going to be the full picture. I think most people in western Sydney understood that and accepted that."

Leto noted that the surrounding road network, including the newly opened M12 motorway, was always expected to carry the bulk of early passenger movements but that it will need to adapt as passenger numbers swell.

The six-station Western Sydney International Airport metro line is expected as early as late 2027, but could be pushed back to mid 2028.

"This is about what's happening over the next 20 — 30 years, not what happens over the next 20 — 30 days," he said. "I think there's going to be more infrastructure that will be required to support the growth of the airport."

Round-the-clock transport will take time to mature, Leto said.

"We've never had a 24-hour airport, so it's a new thing for Sydney to grapple with and understand and learn how to leverage."

However, local government leaders have warned that interim solutions must not displace long-term public transport commitments.

Penrith mayor Todd Carney said the completed metro line to St Marys would eventually be a "gamechanger", but called on the state government to fund the full north-south rail link. The route linking St Marys to Tallawong and Bradfield to Macarthur remains in the early planning stages.

"Ours is one of the fastest-growing regions in the country and with that growth comes enormous opportunity," Carney said. "However, communities can only benefit from opportunity if they can access it.''

The rail delivery timeline blew out after lead contractor Webuild lodged claims for around $2.2 billion in contract variations, slowing station works.

The dispute was compounded when an independent probity investigation uncovered invoicing and payroll irregularities among subcontractors, triggering referrals to the police, the NSW Independent Commission Against Corruption, and the National Anti-Corruption Commission.

Commercial passenger services on the airport metro line are now not expected to run until late 2027 at the earliest, with Premier Chris Minns revealing in June that services may not open until mid 2028.

title: The 'growing' health threat now responsible for one in 10 Australian deaths
text:
In Brief Dementia caused more than 10 per cent of deaths in Australia last year.

The figure increased by almost 40 per cent in the past decade, while deaths due to heart diseases decreased.

Dementia now accounts for more than one in 10 Australian deaths for the first time as advocates warn of a continued surge in the condition as the population ages.

More than 19,000 people (10.1 per cent) died from dementia, including Alzheimer's disease, in 2025, according to analysis released on Tuesday as part of the Australian Bureau of Statistics' (ABS) Causes of Death report.

Dementia has been the leading cause of death for women in Australia since 2016, and in 2024 it overtook cancer and heart disease to become Australia's leading killer nationally.

This is the first time dementia deaths have exceeded 10 per cent, more than double the rates reported in 2006, when dementia was the fourth-leading cause of death nationally.

Dementia Australia's chief executive officer, professor Tanya Buchanan, said the new data reinforced the urgent need to raise awareness of the condition as a leading public health issue affecting Australians.

"The data underlines the critical need for more recognition and funding to support people living with dementia, their families and carers," Buchanan said in a statement.

"Despite the growing impact of dementia, investment in specific services, supports and prevention has not kept the same pace, and the stigma that surrounds dementia continues. This needs to change."

Buchanan said that with nearly 500,000 Australians living with dementia, without "significant intervention", the figure was expected to increase to more than one million by 2065.

A gendered killer

In 2025, women accounted for more than 60 per cent of all deaths attributed to dementia in Australia.

The report found that there were almost twice as many deaths from dementia as from ischaemic heart diseases, which is the second leading cause of death for women.

The ABS said that in 2025, there were just 2,791 deaths separating the top two leading causes of death, with that gap continuing to widen as dementia deaths increase over time, and deaths from ischaemic heart disease continued to decline.

Between 2016 and 2025, the number of deaths due to dementia increased by 37 per cent, while deaths due to ischaemic heart diseases and cerebrovascular diseases decreased by 16.2 per cent and 12.1 per cent, respectively.

The mortality rate for ischaemic heart diseases was the lowest on record since its peak in 1968.

After ischaemic heart diseases and cerebrovascular diseases, lung cancer and chronic lower respiratory diseases rounded the top five leading causes of death, which in 2025 represented more than 30 per cent of all registered deaths.

title: Harry Kane, Alexia Putellas win Ballon d'Or as England ends 25-year wait

In brief Harry Kane is the first Englishman to take home a Ballon d'Or since Michael Owen in 2001.

The long-awaited honour capped a career-defining season for the striker.

Harry Kane has become England's first Ballon d'Or winner in 25 years in his native city of London, beating Lamine Yamal and Kylian Mbappé.

Alexia Putellas claimed the women's prize for a third time to extend Spain's domination of the award, thanks to her role in leading Barcelona to last season's Champions League before moving to London City Lionesses.

The first-ever Ballon d'Or ceremony on English soil got off to an inauspicious start on Tuesday as London traffic caused a nearly hour-long delay, with many of the star names arriving late.

But there was a happy ending for the hometown hero as Kane collected the crowning glory of his career to date, becoming the first Englishman to win the award since Michael Owen in 2001.

The 33-year-old Bayern Munich forward struck a remarkable 73 goals in 65 games for club and country last season, propelling the German giants to a league and cup double.

title: Five years after AUKUS was signed, the first submarine has been named
text:
In brief The first US submarine bound for Australia under AUKUS has been revealed.

Its arrival marks a major milestone in the defence pact.

The United States has revealed the first nuclear submarine that will deploy to Australia under the AUKUS agreement, five years after the $386 billion defence pact was signed.

The USS Colorado, a 10-year-old Virginia-class submarine, will make its new home at Western Australia's HMAS Stirling from late 2027, Defence Minister Richard Marles revealed in a joint statement with his US and British counterparts on Tuesday.

It's the first of up to four US submarines, and one from the UK, set to rotate through the base while Australian Defence Force personnel get to grips with owning and operating nuclear submarines.

But Colorado's arrival in Australia will be controversial because of outrage sparked in late May over revelations that the US would deliver lesser equipment than first promised.

The original AUKUS plans were for Australia to receive two used vessels and a new Virginia-class submarine before building one of its own in Adelaide.

Colorado is a "fast-attack" submarine, reaching speeds of more than 46km/h, compared with Australia's Collins-class subs' underwater top speed of 37km/h.

title: Australians are becoming less convinced about what comes next
text:
Feelings matter. That’s why for over 25 years, the Australian Unity Wellbeing Index has asked Australian adults how satisfied they feel about their lives and life in Australia. It’s a simple but powerful way to understand how we are faring as a country.

This year's index tracked Australians' wellbeing in a challenging year at home and abroad. We also set out to understand how Australians see life playing out for future generations.

More than 10,000 Australians took part in the survey in April and May, just before the federal budget. In September, we went back to almost 1,500 of the same people to see what had changed.

How Australians feel about personal wellbeing in 2026

Compared with 2025, personal wellbeing held steady.

Enter email address Subscribe Morning (Mon–Fri) Afternoon (Mon–Fri) Weekend Insight By subscribing, you agree to SBS’s terms of service and privacy policy including receiving email updates from SBS.

In April–May, the average score on the Personal Wellbeing Index was 67.2 out of 100. This assesses satisfaction across seven areas of personal life:

Standard of living

Health

Achieving in life

Relationships

Safety

Community connectedness

Future security

By September, however, the index had slipped 1.1 points.

Satisfaction with personal safety and future security, which had already dropped in April-May, fell further. Satisfaction with standard of living also declined.

The survey moved from phone to online in 2024. Online scores tend to be lower because people answer differently in private than when speaking to an interviewer. Trends are best read within each survey method.

Feelings about national wellbeing took a hit

We also surveyed people about their feelings about life in Australia more generally, via a different measure we call the National Wellbeing Index. This assesses satisfaction across six areas:

The economic situation

State of the natural environment

Social conditions

Government

Business

National security

Compared to personal wellbeing, Australians' feelings about national wellbeing took a bigger hit. In April-May, the National Wellbeing Index fell 3.2 points from 2025 to 54.8 out of 100.

Last year's survey saw a rise in national wellbeing. This was driven mainly by higher satisfaction with the economy and the government.

This year, however, those were the areas that dropped most, and they hadn’t recovered by September.

Averages can hide who is doing it toughest

Australians experiencing unemployment or those on low incomes reported some of the lowest wellbeing of any population groups.

This gap isn't new. The index has documented it for over 25 years, and it has only meaningfully narrowed once: during the pandemic, when income support payments were doubled.

Young adults are also struggling. We also found that:

56.1 per cent of 18- to 24-year-olds reported high or very high psychological distress

45.7 per cent felt lonely at least some of the time.

How will future Australians fare?

This year we also asked Australians to look ahead.

We asked about five societal challenges that closely map to the transitions identified in the government's latest Intergenerational Report:

Housing costs

Artificial intelligence

Access to healthcare

Climate change

Global political instability

People saw every challenge as hitting future generations harder than themselves.

Housing stood out, with more than four in five (83.4 per cent) believing housing costs would have a high negative impact on future generations.

Younger Australians expect to feel it, too: seven in ten of those aged 18 to 34 expected housing costs to negatively affect their own lives.

The May federal budget included reforms aimed at intergenerational equity, particularly by addressing housing costs and availability.

But when we asked again in September, views on housing hadn't shifted.

What did shift was the share of people expecting AI to negatively impact their lives. This rose 9.3 percentage points in four months, and by 15.1 points among people aged 65 and over.

A vision for the future

We also asked Australians to tell us, in their own words, what kind of Australia they want for future generations.

Across almost 10,000 responses, a broadly shared vision emerged. Australians want a country that is safe and socially connected, environmentally sustainable, fair, affordable and economically secure.

Almost six in ten (58.1 per cent) wrote about at least one of four themes:

Safety

Environmental and climate action

Improved cost of living and financial security

A strong economy

That share held steady regardless of age, income, gender, location, education or language spoken at home. It is a genuine reminder that there is more connection between us than disconnection.

READ MORE The taboo wealth tax debate experts say Australia can no longer ignore

Australians also feel this future is partly theirs to shape; almost two in three (62.7 per cent) said they feel responsible for the wellbeing of future generations.

That's a striking result in these challenging times when, as Treasurer Jim Chalmers recently put it, Australians face a test of whether we "turn on each other" or "change and adapt and reform and prosper together through all of this uncertainty".

But that responsibility doesn’t sit with individuals alone. The challenge for policymakers, communities, and institutions is to match Australians' forward-looking outlook with legislated mechanisms to turn this much needed long-term thinking into reality.

READ MORE Young Australians may keep pace with their parents — but a deeper wealth rift is emerging

The federal government's Measuring What Matters framework already tracks much of what Australians described to us, from safety and sustainability to financial security and a strong economy.

But measuring wellbeing isn't the same as acting on it, and there’s currently no mechanism to ensure the framework is used in decision-making.

Australians have been clear about the country they want to hand on. Now we need to make sure the decisions that shape it are measured against that vision.

A council whose mayor resigned on Wednesday morning has held a bizarre press conference, with the chief executive saying she did not know the mayor had officially stepped down, and the acting mayor had not read her allegations of bullying. Jos Mitchell resigned from her role at Redlands City Council, on Brisbane’s bayside, alleging it was a toxic workplace that had a detrimental impact on her health. Mitchell had been on sick leave since May, and in a statement said she had recently undergone surgery and was suffering from an autoimmune disease. Deputy Mayor Julie Talty and council CEO Louise Rusan initially said the mayor had not officially resigned. Julius Dennis Deputy Mayor Julie Talty, who had been acting mayor while Mitchell was on leave, fronted media with Redlands chief executive Louise Rusan at 11.30am, insisting it was business as usual for the council.

“We understand there’s been some statements in the media by our mayor, Jos Mitchell, in regards to her intention to resign her position,” Talty said. “At this stage, we’ve not had any formal confirmation of that, so we’ll continue to support the mayor until she does give us that confirmation.” Jos Mitchell had been on leave since May 11. Dan Peled Talty said she had not read the comments made by Mitchell online, so she could not speak to them. Rusan began her statement by saying it was “business as usual” at the council, but was pressed by journalists about screenshots of an email sent to her by Mitchell tendering her resignation at 5am.

She was pulled to the side by an adviser before returning to the microphones. “I’ve just received advice that we’ve received a resignation, right this moment,” Rusan said. “So up until two seconds ago, I had not had any contact with the mayor.” Rusan insisted the council had a “wonderful” culture, but would not speak directly about the allegations by Mitchell of a smear campaign. “I believe we have a very good culture here at Redland City Council,” she said.

An hour and a half after the presser, the council put out an official media release acknowledging Mitchell’s resignation. “The Office of Mayor at Redland City Council has become vacant, triggering a by-election to elect a new Mayor of Redland City,” it read. The strange press conference took place outside the council building. Matt Dennien It said Talty would remain as acting mayor until a by-election was held by the Electoral Commission of Queensland. “On behalf of Council, I wish the former mayor all the best for the future,” Talty said.

Staff wrapped up the press conference before she could take questions on the claims of bullying and stalking. Speaking in parliament on Wednesday afternoon, local government minister Ann Leahy said her department would work with the commission to organise an election. She ensured that it would not occur during the Christmas period, but didn’t clarify if the vote would be held sooner, or pushed into next year. Ann Leahy addressed the situation in parliament. Jamila Filippone “A key priority throughout this process is to ensure the residents of the Redlands community have a local government that works for them,” Leahy said.

A nationwide review of biosecurity measures will target the imported red fire ant incursion in Sydney’s inner west after revelations the location of the nest was only required to be checked every three years. A biosecurity control order is in place to limit the movement of high-risk goods after the established fire ant nest was discovered in Enfield Intermodal Logistics Centre in September, and the public was notified two weeks ago. The established fire ant nest was discovered under concrete. NSW Government A review by the inspector-general of biosecurity will examine the Sydney nest as a first case study in a broad assessment of biosecurity policies. In the past three years, more than 160 ant lures were deployed around the Enfield site and until September did not detect any fire ants. While some of the businesses at the logistics centre were considered higher risk and monitored more frequently, under current policies the location where the nest was discovered only required checking every three years.

Advertisement

Invasive Species Council advocacy director Reece Pianta said: “The current biosecurity arrangements clearly do not reflect biological reality and they need to be urgently changed.” Pianta said he hoped the review would provide recommendations to strengthen the biosecurity system to prevent fire ants from establishing elsewhere in Australia. Reece Pianta (left) a fire ant expert at the Invasive Species Council, and local resident and fire ants activist Stuart Webber, inspect a fire ants mound in a horse paddock in Queensland. Dan Peled An interim report, to be made public by April, will examine the management of the biosecurity risk at sites such as Enfield, including surveillance arrangements, according to a document outlining the approach of the inspector-general’s review. After the interim report is delivered, the broader review will look at other cases around the country to determine if the current approaches to risk management and information sharing are adequate to protect Australia’s biosecurity.

Advertisement

The Sydney nest is thought to have been more than a year old when it was discovered, and the ants’ country of origin remains unknown. As nests mature in six months, at which point queen ants can fly to other locations, this would have given the ants time to establish themselves in other locations. Related Article Environmental threats ‘It can get worse’: The bite that burns like fire and killed a football hero A control order now covers a two-kilometre radius around the Enfield nest site, which requires businesses that move soil, mulch, turf, potted plants and heavy equipment to take special precautions before transporting the items outside the controlled zone. More than 400 calls from members of the public have been made to the government’s fire ant hotline, but no further signs of the deadly pest have been confirmed. A team of 60 officers and nine sniffer dogs have combed nearby parks, streets and schools and found no further nests. Fire ants are one of the world’s worst invasive species and responsible for at least 80 deaths in the United States.

The painful bite can kill pets and native wildlife and can be deadly for humans sensitive to insect bites. title: Forget the mortgage belt: Gamers are getting smashed and Chalmers should worry

Analysis PoliticsFederalInflation Forget the mortgage belt: Gamers are getting smashed and Chalmers should worry Shane Wright October 28, 2026 — 3:51pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Put aside your pity for those with a mortgage or people struggling to put food on the table. It’s the gamers who are being hit by inflation. And as gamers deal with huge spikes in the prices of their consoles, the policy problems facing the Reserve Bank, Jim Chalmers and the phalanx of state and territory treasurers follow. Chalmers and Finance Minister Katy Gallagher have to use their upcoming budget update to actually reduce spending. Aresna Villanueva The latest monthly inflation figures from the bureau of statistics all-but guaranteed that the Reserve Bank’s monetary policy committee will inflict another rate rise on the economy on Melbourne Cup Day. The 4.3 per cent headline inflation rate for September, and 3.6 per cent for the key underlying measure were, as the bank’s deputy governor Andrew Hauser said, too high.

Advertisement

As Hauser and governor Michele Bullock have often reminded Australians, the RBA has only one tool to deal with inflation. Hence its four rate rises this year, with the big chance of another that will push the cash rate to an 18-year high of 4.85 per cent next Tuesday. By lifting rates, the bank is trying to reduce overall demand across the economy with the stated aim of bringing inflation back to its 2-3 per cent target – something it has spectacularly failed to do since the final days of the Abbott government – by the end of next year. It can definitely be assisted by a reduction in government spending, at the federal and state level. Chalmers and Finance Minister Katy Gallagher have to use their upcoming budget update to actually reduce spending.

Advertisement

No matter how they characterise the pressures on government services, a budget deficit of $31.5 billion (after a $22.3 billion shortfall in 2025-26) is a loosening of monetary policy during a period of excess demand in the economy. Related Article Inflation Inflation jumps to 4.3 per cent, fuelling prospect of Cup Day rate rise Their state counterparts, many of whom seem to believe their job is to ignore their role in the economy while putting out their hands for more federal cash, have to dramatically lift their performances and tighten their belts. They have to make some tough decisions because of two other issues at play and directly outside government control. The first is the war started by Donald Trump against Iran. Brent crude started the year at $US60 a barrel. On Wednesday, it was $US115.

Advertisement

For the past two months, it has averaged above $US100 a barrel. This spike is feeding through the global economy, from bowsers to PVC pipes to agricultural fertilisers, and is one of the reasons that central banks everywhere are lifting their interest rates. The second big factor is the one that is hurting the struggling gamers. The AI construction boom is lifting business investment and pitting tech firms against each other in a semiconductor and chip war. That war has spilt over into the broader economy. The price of the next Nintendo Switch is going to soar. The September inflation figures showed the costs of games and toys have climbed 15.5 per cent over the past 12 months. Only petrol and diesel have gone up by more.

Advertisement

It’s the biggest increase in games and toys on record and is because demand for computer chips in games and consoles is running much, much faster than supply. Prices for computer equipment, which fell 91 per cent through the first 25 years of this century, have climbed by 6.3 per cent over the past 12 months. It’s why the price of a Nintendo Switch 2 has climbed by 10 per cent this year. Why the Sony PS5 is up by 20 per cent. A MacBook Neo by 17 per cent. iPhones and iPads are going up by even more. The inflation figures were released around the same time that SK Hynix, one of the world’s biggest producers of computer chips and semiconductors, released its third quarter earnings report. It showed average selling prices of its key products had climbed by 20 per cent over the past three months and up four-fold since last year. And it’s not going to get any better.

Advertisement

Company chief financial officer Kim Woo-hyun warned huge demand from across the world meant supply shortages were likely to “persist through to 2030”. Gamers will have to go back to playing pick-up-sticks or dust-encrusted versions of Squatter if that comes to pass. Treasury secretary Jenny Wilkinson, who sits on the Reserve Bank’s monetary policy committee, on Wednesday noted that the data centre building boom is competing for labour and resources with government infrastructure projects and the housing sector. We don’t have to go back far in time to see what that situation means for ongoing inflation. Just look at the early 2000s mining boom. Chalmers, Gallagher and Anthony Albanese are now clearly on notice that they have to play a larger role in easing demand in the Australian economy to deal with global inflationary pressures. Aspiring gold producer Forrestania Resources has firmed up another piece of its production puzzle, tabling a new mineral resource estimate for its recently acquired Symes Find gold deposit in Western Australia’s Wheatbelt region. The updated JORC-compliant resource clocks in at 803,600 tonnes grading one gram per tonne (g/t) gold for 25,800 ounces using a 0.5g/t cut-off grade. Forrestania’s Symes Find deposit, located in Western Australia’s Wheatbelt region, is set to provide ore to the Edna May production hub (pictured). The new resource defines what’s left in the ground after previous owner, mid-tier producer Ramelius Resources, mined 42,000 ounces of higher-grade 2.41g/t gold from the deposit’s open pits in 2024. Notably, the ore was trucked 121 kilometres to the Edna May processing plant, which Forrestania now owns. Forrestania acquired the project as part of the package from Ramelius in September. The resource is broken down into 220,000 tonnes at 0.83g/t gold in the high-confidence measured category, 406,900 tonnes at 1.07g/t in the indicated category and 176,700 tonnes at 1.07g/t gold in the inferred category.

Advertisement

‘Symes Find is an excellent example of Forrestania’s strategy of acquiring advanced gold assets within trucking distance of Edna May.’ Forrestania Resources chairman David Geraghty Importantly, more than 75 per cent of the remaining gold ounces sit in the higher-confidence measured and indicated categories, giving Forrestania a solid handle on the deposit’s remaining riches as it pushes ahead with mining studies. The resource update comes as the company ticks off a series of important milestones at the Edna May operation, putting it on a fast track to restart gold production in mid-December. As a tangible sign of confidence in its production readiness, Forrestania has already delivered the first ore from its nearby Johnson Range mine to the Edna May run-of-mine pad. Forrestania Resources chairman David Geraghty said: “Symes Find is an excellent example of Forrestania’s strategy of acquiring advanced gold assets within trucking distance of Edna May. Following successful mining from the deposit, this updated resource confirms a meaningful remaining gold inventory and further strengthens Forrestania’s pipeline of future production opportunities as we move toward first gold at Edna May in December 2026.” The Edna May restart will mark a big step in Forrestania’s strategy to build a leading Western Australian gold business using a classic hub-and-spoke model, underpinned by its two strategic processing hubs. While all eyes are on the imminent Edna May restart, the company is also rapidly pushing ahead with refurbishment of its second hub at Lake Johnston, slated for commissioning and production in early 2027.

Advertisement

Forrestania has been quietly assembling a significant inventory of ore sources to feed its two hubs, building a global mineral resource inventory that now tops two million ounces. The tally includes the recently acquired 223,300-ounce Tampia project along with its Tycho, British Hills and Johnson Range deposits. The company’s restart timetable is emerging against a strong Australian gold backdrop, with spot prices consolidating around a handsome A$6000 per ounce, providing a powerful commercial tailwind for its production ambitions. In other news today, Forrestania has drawn a line in the sand on its takeover of Zenith Minerals, confirming its offer, first launched on June 9, will close at 5pm (AWST) on November 12. The company says it will not extend the now-unconditional offer unless its hand is forced under section 624(2) of the Corporations Act 2001, which provides for an automatic extension in certain circumstances. With 62.04 per cent of Zenith already in its grasp, Forrestania appears firmly in the driver’s seat as it eyes the 90 per cent ownership threshold generally required to pursue compulsory acquisition and lock away another piece of its broader WA gold consolidation strategy. With first ore already on the ground at Edna May and a new parcel of ounces confirmed at Symes Find, Forrestania looks to be methodically de-risking its production plans. As the final pieces fall into place for a pre-Christmas restart at Edna May and Lake Johnston making rapid progress towards its 2027 start-up, the two-hub strategy is edging closer to reality, setting the stage for the company to establish itself as a serious new force in WA’s gold sector. Passengers on a luxury ship touring the world have been told their unexpected final stop is Cambodia after the cruise company suspended operations, citing “extraordinary” fuel costs. Florida-based Villa Vie Residences’ 650-passenger ship Odyssey is now moored in Sihanoukville, Cambodia, and the company “is working with residents to co-ordinate disembarkation and identify temporary living arrangements”, according to a statement on Wednesday AEST. The Villa Vie Odyssey’s luxury odyssey has come to an unexpected end. nna\april.glover While the company is covering lodging and local transportation, it hasn’t provided funding for passengers to depart the country, Villa Vie Founder Mikael Petterson said in a telephone interview. About 200 residents were on board when the disembarkation was ordered, he said. Fuel costs for the company have risen over 300 per cent since the start of the US-Israel war on Iran, Villa Vie Residences said, making the “current operating model extremely challenging”. Per-cabin fuel costs, which have historically averaged about $US1800 ($2557) a month, surged to $US6000 to $US8000, it said.

Advertisement

Passengers baulked at a request to chip in to help cover the cost of fuel to depart Cambodia, Petterson said. The company is now proposing that passengers pay roughly $US500 more a month, in addition to a fuel surcharge, as long as prices remain elevated, he said. The company is also seeking financing to depart the area “quite quickly”, Petterson added. Odyssey has been at sea since October 2024, and it’s not like a typical cruise line. Its passengers either rent, own or rent-to-own cabins on the ship. According to a brochure, cabin prices for permanent residency range from just under $US130,000 to $US440,000 for a suite, with monthly fees of $US2000 to $US10,000. It’s unclear where stranded passengers and staff will go after disembarking in Cambodia. The company press release said it “recognises that this is a difficult and disruptive period for residents, crew members, and employees”. Fuel costs have lifted monthly operating costs by about 50 per cent to $US3 million, Petterson said.

“When the war broke out, nobody expected that war to carry on,” he said. “Everyone saw what happened in Venezuela; it was a hit and run ... if you asked anyone, they expected fuel to be elevated for a month, a few months. When the ceasefire came, that was expected to be the end of it. Now, if you look at what the analytics say, we don’t see the end of this until Trump is out of power.” Travel costs – whether by plane, car or ship – have surged since the Iran conflict spiked the price of oil and the products made from it, including diesel, petrol and jet fuel. Those elevated costs are hitting companies’ bottom lines, feeding into inflation and rippling through the global economy. Passengers could sign up for a permanent berth on the Odyssey for a cool $US130,000. The marine gas oil that powers the Odyssey has surged to $US1339 a metric ton in Singapore, compared with about $US700 before the war. Odyssey has stopped in ports from Tonga to Australia this year and, according to its itinerary last updated eight days ago, was due to end 2026 in India.

“As you flip through these pages, envision yourself sailing on a continuous odyssey where every day promises new horizons, cherished memories, and heartfelt connections,” the brochure says. Since the Iran War began, the ship has tried to reduce fuel consumption by slowing its itinerary and spending more time in port, but the measures did not offset fuel costs, it said. The company is now evaluating restructuring and recapitalisation alternatives over the next sixty days. One of the Odyssey’s interior cabins. “The company cannot simply pass increases of that scale on to residents,” the press release said. High jet fuel prices helped spell Spirit Airlines’ demise this spring, while Royal Caribbean reported on Tuesday that higher oil costs have dampened an otherwise strong quarter.

Sam Walker intends to fulfil the final year of his Roosters deal next season despite the spectacular fallout from the unravelling of his contract negotiations. Contract extension negotiations broke down on Monday when the Roosters pulled their three-year $4.2m extension offer. Club chairman Nick Politis was so incensed that the Walker camp asked for more time – he had been offered $1.2 million per season with a ratchet clause – that it was unclear whether the relationship was still tenable. Loading If the salary cap increased by 25 per cent – which is what most clubs are budgeting for – that would have taken Walker’s wage to $1.5 million. Paying any more than that was not an option for the Roosters, who privately feel the Maroons and Kangaroos playmaker wasn’t in their top-four players this year. Sources not authorised to speak publicly believe Walker sat behind superstars James Tedesco, Mark Nawaqanitawase, Robert Toia and Naufahu Whyte in the club’s talent pecking order.

Despite that sentiment, the Roosters’ offer to Walker – before it was rescinded – would have outstripped what any of the quartet can earn. The Roosters also feel that while Walker justified his million-dollar wage this year, steering them to a premiership behind a stacked forward pack, he still isn’t in the top echelon of NRL players. Roosters half Sam Walker’s future is uncertain. Getty Images Walker, who is in camp with Australia for the World Cup, hasn’t spoken to coach Trent Robinson since his offer was pulled. Given the ill feeling on both sides, it’s highly unlikely the parties will get back to the negotiating table. However, Walker has told those close to him that he intends to report to pre-season training once his Kangaroos commitments and mandated holiday period is completed.

Dearden hasn’t asked for a release from North Queensland, but he has long been linked to a move to Sydney that would suit his partner, who has just given birth to a girl. While Walker’s situation has piqued the interests of rivals, none of them can afford 24-year-old without moving on players. While it’s been suggested Melbourne could target Walker if they lose Cameron Munster, the Storm is still hopeful of retaining their pivot. Perth is armed with a 20 per cent marquee salary cap allowance, and are the beneficiaries of a new rule that says the Bears can have first crack at any player who doesn’t fulfil his contract. However, the incoming franchise still has four roster spots that need to be filled, meaning they couldn’t accommodate Walker unless he is heavily subsidised. Kurtley Beale has been recalled to the Wallabies for the first time in five years after the 37-year-old was selected as a shock replacement for Hunter Paisami in Australia’s spring tour squad. The improbable return of Beale, who last played for the Wallabies on the spring tour in 2021, came as his new Western Force teammate James Ramm also earned a call-up to the Wallabies squad for their four-Test tour of the UK in November. Loading The news of Beale’s recall to the Wallabies came hours after it was revealed the veteran had extended his contract with the Western Force, but only on a very modest, train-and-trial deal for the 2027 season. Paisami was named in the spring tour squad last week but has since informed Wallabies coach Les Kiss he would be withdrawing due to personal reasons, having just moved to Japan with his wife and children to start with the Shizuoka Blue Revs.

Advertisement

Beale, who debuted for the Wallabies in 2009 and has played 95 Tests, will fly from Perth to meet the Wallabies in London next week. Australia’s main squad has gathered in Sydney and departs on Saturday. It’s a remarkable return for Beale, who sat out the 2023 season after being charged with sexual assault. But after being acquitted in early 2024, he returned to rugby with the Force and was even named in Joe Schmidt’s first Wallabies squad. Kurtley Beale playing for the Western Force early this month in the Super Rugby AUS competition. Getty Images However, an Achilles tendon injury suffered playing club rugby scuttled that chance of a Test comeback, but Beale returned again for the Force and has played solidly for the last two years. He was under consideration for the Australia A tour of the US but did not go due to visa issues. If Beale gets another Test cap, he will become the third-oldest Wallaby since World War II, behind Greg Holmes and Tony Miller, who played at the same age of 38 years and 113 days.

Advertisement

Ramm has been called into the Wallabies squad after the 28-year-old signed for the Force earlier this year, following four seasons of strong form for Northampton in the English Premiership. The speedy outside back – who plays both fullback and wing – has been playing for Northland in the New Zealand NPC competition for the last few months, and has been called in to bolster the Wallabies’ back three options. New Wallabies squad member James Ramm playing for Northampton. Getty Images It is not Ramm’s first time in a Wallabies squad, given the former Waratah was picked by Dave Rennie in 2020. He didn’t get a run, and after some injury issues, Ramm then departed Australia to join the Saints at the end of 2022. Ramm’s call-up comes ahead of Dylan Pietsch and Corey Toole, who were both regular starters for the Wallabies last year under Schmidt but have fallen out of favour with Kiss.

“With Hunter’s unavailability we’re excited by what Kurtley can bring to the group,” Kiss said. “He’s got 95 caps worth of Test experience and whilst he will primarily cover inside centre he has the versatility to play a number of positions across the backline. “Kurtley’s also been in great form for the Western Force in Super Rugby Pacific and Super Rugby AUS and is excited to contribute to the environment. Kurtley Beale at Wallabies training in 2024, before injurying his achilles tendon. Getty Images “At the same time, James is a player we’ve kept a keen eye on for a while and his form for Northland has been exceptional in recent times. “He’s someone who knows the UK well, having spent a very successful period with Northampton, and can cover multiple positions across the backline.”

The Wallabies also announced Kalani Thomas will be joining the touring squad as a fourth halfback, given Tate McDermott is on standby to return to Australia for the birth of his first child. Olympic great Ariarne Titmus has revealed she was subjected to thousands of hateful messages after criticising a provocative Sydney Sweeney advertisement, saying she was personally attacked over her appearance for standing up for women’s sport. Last month, Titmus joined a chorus of prominent female athletes condemning an advertisement featuring American actress Sydney Sweeney, who appeared scantily clad alongside various pieces of sporting equipment. Sydney Sweeney poses for her controversial Novig ad, which Olympian Ariarne Titmus has criticised. The advertisement, filmed for US sports prediction platform Novig, played on the company’s “just sports” slogan. The former Australian swimmer described it as “an absolute joke” and “the furthest thing from sport”.

Advertisement

“I can’t describe how infuriated I feel when I watch this,” Titmus wrote on social media. “Not only is it a kick in the face to every woman who has dedicated her life to perfecting her craft, but every woman who enjoys sports for what it really is.” Ariarne Titmus’ Instagram response to the Sydney Sweeney advertising campaign. Instagram Titmus received support from fellow Olympians and other prominent female athletes, many of whom shared their own criticism of the advertisement. Speaking at a Racing NSW media event ahead of Golden Eagle Day at Royal Randwick on Saturday, Titmus said she had no idea her comments, posted while holidaying in Europe, would generate such a fierce reaction.

Advertisement

“I got a lot of messages of support but at the same time, I got thousands of comments and messages of hate. It’s unfortunate,” Titmus told this masthead on Wednesday. “I was just trying to do the right thing and use my platform. Being removed from the swimming team now, I feel I can be a bit more vocal … but I was quite surprised by the reception. “But you know what? I’d do it again. I just think how far we come and how incredible our female athletes are around the world. It didn’t sit very nicely with me. Ariarne Titmus at Royal Randwick Racecourse on Wednesday ahead of Saturday’s Golden Eagle Day. Sitthixay Ditthavong “I was quite lucky throughout my swimming career. I never really got much trolling or hate, and I always felt immense support. It was the first time I felt people were attacking me personally and physically [about] how I looked.” Did it affect her?

Advertisement

“It kind of just goes over my head,” she said. “I know who I am. That’s their problem. A lot of them were probably bots, to be honest. Other women who spoke out about it probably got the same [treatment].” It has been just over a year since Titmus, an eight-time Olympic medallist, world record holder and world champion, announced her retirement from swimming. Ariarne Titmus after winning gold in the 400m freestyle at the 2024 Olympic Games. AP Training to become the best swimmer in the world was taxing, but retirement has hardly meant putting her feet up. The past 12 months have been a whirlwind of flights, sponsor appearances and broadcast commitments as Titmus establishes herself beyond the pool. Titmus, who is launching her book Relentless next week, has also partnered with Youngcare to raise awareness of the charity’s work helping young Australians with complex and permanent physical disabilities live independently.

Advertisement

Golden Eagle Day has become one of Australia’s biggest race days, with about $1 million donated to charities each year. For Titmus, the association with racing is fitting. Long before she became a swimming superstar, horses were her first love. She grew up riding them on her family’s property in Tasmania before committing to the pool. Ariarne Titmus with inaugural Golden Eagle winner Kolding at Royal Randwick. Sitthixay Ditthavong With the 2028 Los Angeles Olympics less than two years away, Titmus insists there is no temptation to make a comeback. “The chapter is well and truly closed,” Titmus said. “Zero part of me wanted to be in the water [at the recent Commonwealth Games in Glasgow]. I felt so removed from that team. Every day that’s passed since I’ve retired, I know that it’s the right one.

“I haven’t slowed down. I really thought that it might have a bit of a lull, but I’ve just thrown myself into as much as I possibly can, and the work’s been coming.” Titmus is also preparing for the release of her autobiography on Tuesday, which promises a warts-and-all account of her extraordinary career and the demanding methods of longtime coach Dean Boxall. Their partnership delivered Olympic gold medals and world records, but although it was not always smooth sailing, there was always mutual respect. “I don’t regret one second of it or how hard I pushed myself. It’s definitely a feel-good story,” Titmus said.

“We had big blow-ups. He used to call me a ‘self-cleaning carpet’ because we’d have a big blow-up and then I come back the next day like nothing happened. “In the hard times or the blow-ups – and in the moments where he was pushing me to the brink – I really made sure it was well known that that’s what I wanted from him. I knew that I thrive with that bad cop on my back.”

The Coalition’s proposal to convert Long Bay jail into 12,000 homes has erupted into a fight over the future of housing in prime Sydney locations, with Planning Minister Paul Scully labelling it a fantasy. As Opposition Leader Kellie Sloane questioned why a prison occupied 50 hectares of prime real estate in Sydney’s eastern suburbs, Scully decried the plan as “nothing more than a multibillion-dollar bill to the taxpayer masquerading as a housing plan”. (From left) Maroubra MP and Attorney-General Michael Daley, Planning Minister Paul Scully, and Corrections Minister Anoulack Chanthivong outside Long Bay jail on Wednesday. Sitthixay Ditthavong The housing battle has turned personal after the Coalition and Labor each released plans for massive redevelopments in safe seats held by the opposing party: Woollahra and Edgecliff in Sloane’s seat of Vaucluse, and the Long Bay plan in Attorney-General Michael Daley’s seat of Maroubra. Hours after this masthead revealed the Liberals’ plan to establish a delivery authority to organise the closure of Long Bay prison within 100 days if elected in March, three Labor ministers stood outside the corrections centre on Wednesday to condemn the proposal as unworkable.

Advertisement

“What we’ve seen from the member for Vaucluse and the Liberal Party is a plan to not have housing in Woollahra. This is a distraction and a fantasy of an idea,” Scully said. “The reality is the idea of putting 12,000 homes on the site behind us would create an area of around three times the density of Green Square without any of the transport infrastructure. This doesn’t pass the most basic of planning tests.” The jail houses about 1200 inmates, but the Liberals say there is space for about 12,000 dwellings. Sitthixay Ditthavong Daley said the proposed uplift in density was unworkable given Anzac Parade – the only road in or out of the peninsula – was already “chock-a-block” in the morning. Premier Chris Minns has previously said the only way to make the redevelopment stack up is by building a metro station nearby, which the government has no plans to do. Scully said there were several unanswered questions about the Coalition proposal, including where the jail’s 1200 inmates would be rehoused, and the overall cost. Sloane has suggested selling the land to developers could yield the government up to $2 billion.

Opposition planning spokesman Chris Rath accused the government of claiming they were pro-housing while rejecting each of the Coalition’s three planning proposals, including building 10,000 new homes in the inner west and 10,000 new homes in Camellia-Rosehill. Related Article Exclusive

NSW State Parliament NSW Liberals abandon YIMBY truce as housing goes on the ballot “So they talk a big game on housing, but when it comes to actually delivering, they are 40 per cent behind their National Housing Accord target. In an interview with ABC Sydney on Wednesday morning, Sloane was unable to say what the proposed cost of the redevelopment would be, nor where Long Bay’s 1200 inmates would be rehoused if the proposal went ahead. She argued a delivery authority would be established to work through those issues. Sloane acknowledged the plan would require upgraded transport infrastructure “down the track”, suggesting the extension of the light rail down Anzac Parade was an idea. Cricket Australia chief executive Todd Greenberg has revealed he is in “deep conversations” with national selectors about regenerating an ageing Test team, as it emerged contract discussions with coach Andrew McDonald had also opened. Speaking after Wednesday’s CA annual general meeting, where the organisation revealed it had taken a combined $20 million hit because of a pair of two-day Ashes Tests last summer, Greenberg said he was aware selection chairman George Bailey and his panel had tough decisions to make. Coach Andrew McDonald and chairman of selectors George Bailey will need to usher new players in to the Test team. ICC via Getty Images The futures of Steve Smith, 37, Nathan Lyon, 38, Scott Boland, 37, Mitchell Starc, 36, Josh Hazlewood, 35, and skipper Pat Cummins, 33, who have been central to a largely winning era, are up for debate, while Marnus Labuschagne, 32, is fighting for his Test future in the ongoing third and final Test against South Africa in Cape Town. Greenberg has just returned from South Africa, where selection, particularly heading into Newlands, had been contentious, with three players dropped, and Smith out because of injury.

“Yes, we are in deep conversations about how this team will look and operate over the next six, 12, 18, 24 months,” Greenberg said. Related Article Analysis

But we have an eye on what that looks like after they finish their playing days. We don’t know when that will be but, of course, we’ve got to have an eye on what the transition looks like.” After a home Test summer against New Zealand, Australia have heavy-duty tours of India and England to negotiate. McDonald, who boasts a fantastic record since replacing Justin Langer in 2022, is contracted until the end of next year’s World Cup in South Africa. An industry source, not authorised to speak publicly, said McDonald’s focus was on the current tour, but he was “open” to coaching on. He’s held in incredibly high regard by the Cricket Australia board and by all of us,” Greenberg said. “I think he’s done an outstanding job, and I think his results tell you that. But in saying that, there’s also an eye of what’s coming next, and there’s, no doubt, that there’ll be a transition of this team, and we want to make sure that we can have oversight of that so that we protect and thrive into the next phase, whoever that might be.” Mike Baird resigned from his role at Cricket Australia last month, but still insists BBL privatisation is the best way forward. Getty Outgoing chairman Mike Baird presided over his final AGM, having last month lost the support of his home state, Cricket NSW, to carry on as a director, amid ructions over plans to privatise BBL clubs. However, David Boon, who assumed the role of interim chair on Wednesday following Baird’s official departure, declared the sport’s governing body would plough on with the contentious plans that have attracted interest from up to 30 Indian, European and US-based entities, who have had access to a data room.

title: The four balls that turned the Test, and saved captain Pat Cummins
text:

SportCricketAustralian cricket The four balls that turned the Test, and saved captain Pat Cummins Andrew Wu October 28, 2026 — 3:08pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Mitchell Starc’s devastating burst on the shadow of stumps not only saved his captain but also his team. A day in which Australia were behind from the moment Pat Cummins sent South Africa in to bat finished with honours shared after Starc’s match-turning four wickets in the space of six deliveries. Mitchell Starc rescued Australia on Tuesday in Cape Town. AP Photo/Halden Krog Only those in the camp can honestly answer if the visitors would have settled for a Proteas total of 329 if offered before the day, but such a scoreline would have been gleefully accepted when openers Aiden Markram and Marques Ackerman destroyed the new ball. So dominant were they in reaching 0-158, Cummins’ decision to bowl first was rivalling that of former England captain Nasser Hussain, whose infamous call to send Australia in at the Gabba in 2002 resulted in a stumps score of 2-364.

Advertisement

The hosts were still in control when Cummins handed Starc a second brand-new Kookaburra about 20 minutes before stumps. Related Article Updated

Australian cricket Cricket Australia boss has ‘deep conversations’ with selectors about Test team At 6-325, a score of 400-plus was on the cards for the Proteas, who had wicketkeeper Ryan Rickelton and damaging all-rounder Marco Jansen settled at the crease and another of their lower-order tormentors from Gqeberha, Simon Harmer, padded up in the pavilion. Hours earlier in the first session, Starc – and Australia’s vaunted quicks – repeatedly found the middle of the bat. Now, his golden left arm was launching missiles that curved wickedly late to smash pads and stumps. Starc, who had seen Travis Head drop a dolly, did not need his teammates. His final four victims were all out bowled or lbw.

Advertisement

Shortly after tea, Starc had the unflattering figures of 0-62 from 12 overs. By the close of play, he had taken his 20th bag of five or more wickets, his analysis of 6-72 his seventh-best return in his 110-Test career. Of his eight best figures, six have come in his past two years. Age is not wearying him. 80.4 overs, Ryan Rickelton lbw b Starc 42 (South Africa: 7-327) After capturing his first two wickets with bouncers on a surface not offering much lateral movement off the seam, Starc made the pitch just about a non-factor. Armed with the second new ball, Starc aimed full and straight to Rickelton, who had provided the ballast in an ominous 95-run stand with the damaging Jansen.

Advertisement

The yorker straightened and swung extremely late, thudding into the back pad of Rickelton, who had been squared up by a delivery he attempted to play through mid-wicket when a fuller face of the bat was needed. A despondent, and defeated, Rickelton accepted his fate without asking the video umpire for salvation. 80.6 overs, Marco Jansen b Starc 52 (South Africa: 8-328) Jansen was the pick of Starc’s wickets, dismissed by a 143.6 km/h thunderbolt that was reminiscent of his delivery to New Zealand great Brendon McCullum in the 2015 World Cup final.

Advertisement

Having spent the best part of two hours at the crease for his 52, Jansen’s eye was well and truly in, but he was beaten for pace and swing. He played late and down the wrong line, unable to jam his bat down on a ball to prevent it from clattering into the base of his off stump. 82.1 overs, Gerald Coetzee b Starc 0 (South Africa 9-329) With a Test average of 13.40, Gerald Coetzee is no bunny with the bat, so it’s understandable why his partner Simon Harmer did not attempt to shield the No.10 from Starc. He should have. The man who made a career-best 82 last week did not face another ball.

Advertisement

After seeing his more skilled teammates fired out by Starc’s yorkers, Coetzee did not want his toes near the ball first up. He backed away slightly to a 144.1 km/h full delivery, which ricocheted off his front pad into the stumps for a golden globe. 82.3 Kagiso Rabada lbw b Starc 0 (South Africa 329 all out) There was no disgrace in Kagiso Rabada’s dismissal, trapped plumb in front to almost the identical delivery that removed Rickelton minutes earlier. If a top-six batter with a Test average of nearly 50 could not defend it, then what hope for a No.11?

Advertisement

Related Article Analysis

Australian cricket Resilient Starc and Lyon laugh last, but Australia’s biggest mountain awaits Starc’s timing could not have been better. By completing his rout with less than 10 minutes before stumps, he spared Australia’s openers a nervy over or two in fading light. Thanks to Starc, Australia are back in the game. Now comes the hard part. They have to bat. News, results and expert analysis from the weekend of sport sent every Monday. Sign up for our Sport newsletter.

Hastings Technology Metals has completed a 49 per cent acquisition of the Kabin Buri hydrometallurgical processing plant in Thailand, as the company fast-tracks its transition from miner to rare earths downstream producer. The US$15 million (A$21.3 million) deal sees Hastings take a significant stake in the Thai facility’s owner, with a significant portion of the payment tied to performance. The consideration includes a previously paid US$0.5 million cash deposit and US$8 million in equity, to be satisfied through the issue of 23 million Hastings shares at an agreed price of 50 cents apiece to its partner, Enuo Holdings. First feedstock shipment arriving at Hastings’ Kabin Buri hydrometallurgical rare earths plant in Thailand last quarter. A further US$1 million is payable as a commissioning payment, with the final US$5.5 million in deferred cash consideration payable only when contractual production and sales performance milestones are met. The company says work is already progressing at the facility to upgrade its planned nameplate output capacity to 12,000 tonnes per annum of mixed rare earth chloride (MREC), representing a doubling of the plant’s originally contemplated throughput.

Advertisement

‘Completion gives us a clear run at construction and commissioning, with feedstock contracted.’ Hastings Technology Metals chief executive officer Vince Catania Hastings says testing and commissioning are on track to kick off in the first quarter, with first production expected to follow shortly after. Importantly, the company says it has de-risked the plant’s start-up phase by securing a binding feedstock supply agreement with Enuo for a minimum of 10,000 tonnes per annum of monazite concentrate. The supply is expected to come from Africa, giving Hastings an independent source of feed while its flagship Yangibana project in Western Australia is brought online to potentially provide a longer-term runway for the plant’s initial years of operation. Hastings Technology Metals chief executive officer Vince Catania said: “Completion gives us a clear run at construction and commissioning, with feedstock contracted. Our job now is to get on-spec product out of the door by Q2 2027.” The acquisition accelerates Hastings’ mine-to-market strategy, transforming the Kabin Buri facility into a significant processing hub. The plant chemically cracks and leaches monazite concentrate into mixed rare earth chloride (MREC), an intermediate product for specialist rare earths separation plants.

It is one of the rare earth industry’s most technically demanding processing steps and, with only a handful of operators able to do it successfully, has become one of the sector’s biggest barriers to entry. Based on management’s indicative estimates, the now-expanded plant could generate US$110.4 million (A$158M) in gross annual revenue and US$35.7 million (A$51.5M) in profit before tax at full capacity. Hastings’ share of that profit is forecast at US$15.5 million (A$22.35M) in the first full year of production, followed by US$17.5 million (A$25.2M) thereafter. Looking ahead, Hastings has begun preparing an investment promotion application with Thailand’s Board of Investment (BOI). If successful, the promotion could allow the plant to be majority foreign-owned, opening the door for Hastings to increase its stake from the current 49 per cent. It could also provide significant tax incentives, including a corporate income tax exemption for up to 13 years. By picking up a near-term production asset in Thailand, Hastings has found a shortcut to cash flow and skipped the long lead times that stall so many aspiring miners. Its Yangibana project remains the main event, but the Thai plant is a handy stepping stone towards a place among the world’s downstream players. Richard Tognetti, the artistic director and lead violin of the Australian Chamber Orchestra, seems remarkably chill for someone who’s “working frantically”, as he puts it. Currently wrapping up the ACO’s 50th anniversary with a national tour of Beethoven’s Pastoral (aka Symphony No. 6), his mind’s already deep in the orchestra’s program for 2027, which will be led by Johann Sebastian Bach’s St John Passion. “It’s simply one of the greatest works ever conceived by humankind,” says Tognetti from his beachside home in Manly. “J.S. Bach is widely believed by anyone who cares to know about such things these days as the greatest composer, and his two surviving passions – the St Matthew and St John – are regarded as these extraordinary musical events. It’s going to be a pretty good year.” Richard Tognetti, the Australian Chamber Orchestra’s artistic director and lead violin, regrets the stupidity of our politicians. Georges Antoni Worst habit? Impatience. I’ve always got 15 plates in the air and way too many projects, so I’m always lying awake at night, worrying about things I need to get done. As technology gets faster, our impatience gets worse, which is ridiculous. So recently, I set myself up with a turntable hi-fi system. It’s vinyl-only, and you’re only allowed to use it if you listen to a whole side of a record.

Advertisement

Greatest fear? The shark problem. Surfing is my life. I grew up in Wollongong, and I’ve been surfing since I was a kid. So, as a surfer, my greatest fear is that the shark problem is going to become so unmanageable that we’ll become a Reunion Island “paradise” with no swimming or surfing. Unfortunately, it’s become a highly politicised issue. The trolling on the internet is almost a joke. It’s people who don’t even know what the ocean is saying, “Well, you deserve to die because you’re in their backyard.” There’s a lot of misinformation and emotional anxiety, and what we’re left with is a lot of fear and distress in the surfing and ocean swimming community. The line that has stayed with you? “Art makes grand our own stupid lives.” Seven dangerous words. I think I got it from Clive James’ amazing book, Cultural Amnesia. It’s self-explanatory but it means that art – which is everywhere – elevates you in a way that makes you feel the world is more interesting than it actually is.

Advertisement

The more we can be involved in cultural pursuits, the better off we are. At the least, it keeps us out of trouble. If a kid plays a clarinet and they’re obsessed with playing it well, it focuses the brain, you get emotional expression, it brings joy to people. Art does that. It’s interesting that there’s a lot of talk about saving Western culture these days, but most of the people who make us paranoid about it are those who don’t even consider its merits. I wish politicians would read more. I was involved in a rather narky incident with a very well-known politician who told me they don’t have time to read, and I just thought, “Therein lies the problem.” Tognetti began playing violin at the age of five: “It takes years just to get a reasonable sound,” he says. Georges Antoni Biggest regret? I think it was Helen Mirren who was once asked this and she said, “I didn’t tell enough people to f--- off.” [laughs] Well, we all know what she means. But I suppose my biggest regret at my age is that I’ve tried so hard to convince politicians about the value of music education and to this day, I regret that more of them haven’t listened. It’s shithouse, totally depressing, and if anything they’re making it worse.

Advertisement

It’s a no-brainer, learning how to read and write and appreciate music. And not just Mozart, but lots of different types of music. Have you ever met someone who said, “I learned to play the guitar when I was young and I really regret it”? No! So I regret I couldn’t convince these people. I take full responsibility for the stupidity of politicians. Tell us about your turning point. When you start playing piano as a kid, if you just work at it a bit, with one note you can make as good a sound as any pianist who’s ever lived. With a violin, no way! It takes years just to get a reasonable sound. I think it was in 1974 in Wollongong. I would’ve been about eight. I remember standing on a stage and playing my own little pathetic piece and just thinking, “Wow, I can actually kind of play.” That was a turning point. I started playing violin when I was five. The worst thing I hear is parents saying about their kids, “Oh my God, it sounds like shit.” Yeah, we know it sounds like shit… until it doesn’t!

Advertisement

What is the song you wish was yours? The last movement of Symphony No. 41 by Wolfgang Amadeus Mozart, which is nicknamed the “Jupiter Symphony” for good reason. As incredible as Bach is, and possibly we could all agree that he’s the greatest composer, here is Mozart bringing together tunes from the street, opera tunes, ecclesiastical melodies and balancing, like, seven of them at one time so that all you’ve got is pure exhilaration. That for me is, wow. If I wrote that, I’d be like, yep, that’ll do. And then the poor bastard goes and dies at 35! It was one of the last things he wrote. If you could time travel, where would you choose to go? The fairly sophisticated times of Mozart’s Vienna. Which is nothing like modern-day Vienna. As much as the modern-day Viennese musicians will have you believe they’re connected to Mozart, they’re not in any way or form.

title: Twin brothers win Lotto twice in two years
text:
Twin brothers have defied the odds and are planning to hit the road after they celebrated their second lotto win within two years.

The Albany brothers, 65, from Western Australia's Great Southern, shared a $1m Millionaire Medley prize within two years of winning Set For Life.

The first win helped them buy their sister's home, now they can pay off the property and hit the road.

Both winning tickets were purchased from Clark's Newsagency in Albany.

One of the lucky brothers said he bought the ticket after his dentist appointment was cancelled.

"When I got home, I realised I'd bought a Slikpik and forgotten to get my usual numbers as well," he said.

"I wouldn't usually ever buy more than one ticket a day, but when I realised I'd only bought the Slikpik, I thought I'd pop back because I like playing the same numbers.

"I know it's completely random, but it's what I like to do."

The second trip to the retailer resulted in a System 8 entry that secured the $1 million prize.

"We're set now," one brother said.

"We've worked physically demanding jobs our whole lives but now we can relax a bit more, pay the house off and then we both want to get caravans so we can travel around Australia together."

The twin brothers have won Lotto twice within two years.

While one brother is dreaming of life on the road, the other has already celebrated in his own way.

"I bought myself a watch because you have to treat yourself a bit," he said.

"I also like disco and dancing, so I might celebrate with my girlfriend."

"Winning a major prize is a memorable moment for any player, but to experience two significant wins within such a short period is remarkable," she said.

"It's wonderful to see these brothers using their prizes to secure their future and enjoy retirement together."
